lessons.title: Hash maps and sets: lookup interfaces
lessons.summary: A map associates a value with a key; a set remembers only whether a key is present.
lessons.body:
A map associates a value with a key; a set remembers only whether a key is present. Before using either, decide whether the query is exact membership or an ordered search.

Suppose you have a list of a million customer IDs and you need to check, for each of a million incoming orders, whether the customer exists. Scanning the list each time costs up to a million comparisons per order: a million orders times a million comparisons is around 10¹² (a million million) operations in total. Sorting the list and binary searching cuts each check to about 20 comparisons, because each comparison halves the range still to search and 2²⁰ is about a million.

A **hash table** does better still: on average, each check takes a constant number of steps, no matter how many IDs you store. This makes hash maps and sets useful for many everyday lookup tasks.

## The idea in one picture

A hash table is an array of **hash buckets** (or slots). To store a key, you run it through a **hash function** that turns it into an integer, then reduce that integer to an array index.

```
key "alice"
   |
   v
hash("alice") = 8,413,776,201
   |
   v  mod 8 (array size)
index 1

 0     1        2     3     4  ...
[ ]  [alice]  [ ]   [bob]  [ ]
```

The full hash in the drawing is made up for illustration; Python's real string hash changes from run to run. What matters is the last step: its remainder after dividing by eight is one, so "alice" goes in bucket 1.

To look the key up later, you hash it again, jump straight to the same index and check whether it is there. You never scan the whole array; at most you check the few keys that landed in the same place.

Two different keys can land on the same index. That is a **hash collision**, and every hash table needs a strategy for it (Collision resolution). As long as collisions are rare, each bucket holds about one key and operations stay fast. The "constant on average" promise therefore rests on three assumptions: hashes spread keys evenly, the table is not allowed to get too full, and hashing or comparing one key takes bounded time.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a post room's mail slots
> A post room sorts letters into wall-mounted slots using a fixed rule, say the first letter of the surname. To find someone's post you apply the rule and look in one slot, rather than searching every letter in the building.
>
> **How it maps:** the rule is the hash function plus the reduction to an index, each slot on the wall is a bucket, and two people whose surnames share a first letter are a collision: you check the names inside that one slot.
>
> **Where it stops:** first letters are a poor hash, because surnames bunch up under common letters. A real hash function spreads keys almost evenly, and a hash table adds slots automatically as it fills, which a post room cannot do.

## The interface

There are two flavours.

A **hash map** (dictionary, associative array) stores key → value pairs. In the table below, n is the number of keys stored, and O(1) means "a constant number of steps, however large n gets" (Big-O notation, from the Complexity module):

| Operation | Python | Average |
|---|---|---|
| Insert / update | `d[k] = v` | O(1) |
| Look up | `d[k]`, `d.get(k)` | O(1) |
| Membership | `k in d` | O(1) |
| Delete | `del d[k]` | O(1) |
| Iterate | `for k in d` | O(n) for compact state; retained holes can add work |

A **hash set** stores keys only, and answers "have I seen this?":

```python
seen = set()
# Store membership, without a value.
seen.add("alice")
"alice" in seen      # True
seen.discard("bob")  # no error if absent
```

Sets also support set union (`a | b`), set intersection (`a & b`) and set difference (`a - b`). An intersection iterates over the smaller set and probes the larger one, so on average its cost grows with the size of the *smaller* set only: intersecting a 10-item set with a million-item set takes about 10 lookups.

Other languages have the same pair: Java's `HashMap` / `HashSet`, C++'s `std::unordered_map` / `std::unordered_set` and Go's built-in `map`. JavaScript's Map / Set offer similar interfaces, but the ECMAScript specification only requires average sublinear access (faster than scanning everything), not a particular hash-table representation.

> [!tip] Python dicts remember insertion order
> Since Python 3.7, iterating over a dict returns keys in the order they were first inserted. This is a language guarantee, not an accident. Sets make no such promise: their iteration order depends on the hashes.

A useful consequence: `dict.fromkeys(items)` makes each item a key. A repeated item updates the existing entry without moving it, so `list(dict.fromkeys(items))` gives the distinct items in first-appearance order. It removes duplicates while keeping the input order; it does not sort.

## Key takeaways
- A map stores key–value pairs; a set stores membership.
- Exact-key access is fast on average under well-distributed hashes and bounded-cost keys.
- Dict iteration preserves insertion order; sets offer no such ordering promise.

## Further reading
- [Time complexity of Python operations — Python wiki](https://wiki.python.org/moin/TimeComplexity)
- [Mapping types: dict — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#mapping-types-dict)

lessons.title: Hash-table average and worst cases
lessons.summary: Average O(1) depends on the load factor and an even hash spread; colliding keys make lookups linear and bulk inserts quadratic.
lessons.body:
A hash table's "O(1)" is a conditional promise, not a latency guarantee. Keep three costs apart: hashing and comparing a key, the collision work inside the table, and the occasional resize.

## Average case versus worst case

The O(1) figure is an **average**, and it rests on an assumption: the hash function spreads keys roughly evenly across buckets.

How full a table is matters more than how big it is. The **load factor** measures that fullness: the average number of keys per bucket.

```formula essential
α = n / m
where
α: alpha, the load factor: the average number of keys per bucket, a plain number with no unit (0.75 means three keys for every four buckets)
n: the number of keys currently stored in the table
m: the number of buckets (slots) in the table's array
In words: the load factor is keys divided by buckets. Twelve keys in sixteen buckets is 0.75: the table is three-quarters full, whatever its absolute size.
```

Tables keep α below a fixed limit (Java's `HashMap` uses 0.75, Python's dict about 2/3) by growing the array when it fills up. With α held below a constant, the expected work per operation is constant, whether the table holds ten keys or ten million. This relies on the hash function spreading keys evenly; it says nothing about a bad hash or a deliberate attack.

The **worst case** is very different. If every key hashes to the same bucket, a list-chained table degenerates into one long chain; an unsuccessful lookup or a hit at the end may scan all n keys:

```
 0     1     2              3
[ ]  [ ]   [k1->k2->...->kn] [ ]
```

That makes a lookup O(n). Inserting n keys is worse, because each new key is first compared with every key already in the chain (to check it is not a duplicate). The first key is compared with nothing, the second with one key, the third with two, and so on.

```formula reference
C = n (n − 1) / 2
where
C: the total number of key comparisons needed to insert n distinct keys into one shared chain
n: the number of keys inserted
In words: the comparisons add up to roughly half of n squared, so doubling the number of colliding keys roughly quadruples the total work. That growth is written O(n²).
```

For 1,000 colliding keys that is about half a million comparisons, where a good hash needs about 1,000 steps. This happens in practice when:

- the hash function is poor for your data (for example, hashing integers that are all multiples of the table size), or
- an attacker deliberately sends keys that collide, a **hash flooding** attack (Hash flooding and runtime randomisation).

There is also an occasional slow insert: when the table grows, every key is re-inserted into a bigger array, which costs O(n). Spread over all the inserts this averages out to O(1) per insert, which is called **amortised** O(1) (Rehashing and geometric growth).

> [!note] What "O(1) average" really means
> It is the expected cost under a reasonable hash function, ignoring the occasional resize. Hashing the key itself is not free: computing an uncached hash of a string of L characters ordinarily scans all L of them, so it costs O(L). CPython caches string hashes, and identity shortcuts can avoid equality scans; a repeated lookup using the same long string need not rescan it.

## Key takeaways
- Load factor measures keys per bucket rather than total table size.
- Colliding chains can make each operation linear and a sequence of inserts quadratic.
- Hash computation, equality and resizing are separate parts of the cost model.

## Further reading
- [Hash table — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_table)
- [Time complexity of Python operations — Python wiki](https://wiki.python.org/moin/TimeComplexity)

questions.prompt: A chained hash table uses a broken hash function that sends every key to bucket 0. Each insert scans the chain to check the key is not already present. Loading 10,000 distinct keys takes 2 seconds, almost all of it in those comparisons. Roughly how long will loading 20,000 distinct keys take?

options.text: About 2 seconds
options.explanation: That would be true only if each insert cost a constant amount. With every key in one chain, each new key is compared with all the keys already there, so per-insert cost keeps growing.

options.text: About 3 seconds
options.explanation: Three seconds would mean doubling the keys adds only half as much work again, which is less than linear growth. Here the shared chain only gets longer, so each later insert costs more than each earlier one and the total must more than double.

options.text: About 8 seconds
options.explanation: Correct. The total comparisons grow with roughly half the square of the key count, so doubling the keys roughly quadruples the work: from about 50 million to about 200 million comparisons.

options.text: About 4 seconds
options.explanation: Doubling would be right if the total work grew linearly. Here every key is compared with every earlier key, so there are about four times as many pairs, not twice as many.

questions.workedExample:
1. All keys share one bucket, so the table behaves like one linked list.
2. Inserting a key compares it with every key already present. The first key costs nothing, the last costs nearly n comparisons, and the average is about n/2.
3. So the total is about n²/2 comparisons for n keys. Doubling n doubles both the number of inserts and the average chain each one scans: about four times the work.
4. Two seconds therefore becomes about eight. With a working hash, the same load would grow linearly, and the absolute times would be far smaller.
5. This quadratic blow-up is exactly what hash flooding attacks exploit.

questions.prompt: Which statements about hash table performance are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Computing an uncached string hash by scanning all characters costs proportionally to its character count
options.explanation: Correct. Hashing a string that is not already cached means reading every character, so the work grows in proportion to the string's length (Θ(L) for a string of L characters). CPython caches each string object's hash, so a later lookup with the same string object can skip that scan.

options.text: Every individual insert is guaranteed O(1)
options.explanation: An insert that triggers a resize re-inserts all n keys, costing O(n). Inserts are O(1) amortised, not each guaranteed.

options.text: The average O(1) cost relies on the load factor staying below a constant
options.explanation: Correct. Tables grow when keys ÷ buckets passes a limit (0.75 in Java), keeping the expected bucket size constant.

options.text: If all keys collide, a lookup can cost O(n)
options.explanation: Correct. A collision chain or long probe sequence can require linear work in a basic table; tree-bin and other mitigations can change this bound.

options.text: Lookups get faster as you add more keys, because the table grows
options.explanation: Growth only restores the load factor to its previous range; it does not make lookups faster than O(1). Larger tables can be slightly slower due to cache misses.

questions.workedExample:
1. An uncached full string hash ordinarily takes linear character work; cached hashes and identity shortcuts change repeated lookup cost.
2. Individual inserts can trigger expensive resizing.
3. Expected constant table work assumes suitable hash distribution and bounded load.
4. Basic tables can have linear collision-heavy lookups.
5. Growth restores load headroom; it does not guarantee progressively faster queries.

lessons.title: Hashable keys and equality
lessons.summary: The equality contract determines which entries a dictionary treats as the same key.
lessons.body:
The equality contract determines which entries a dictionary treats as the same key. A key is not safe merely because a call to hash succeeds: its equality-relevant state must also remain stable while stored.

## Keys must be hashable

A hash table finds a key by recomputing its hash. If a key's hash could change after insertion, the table would look in the wrong bucket and the entry would be lost. So the contract is:

1. If `a == b`, then `hash(a) == hash(b)`. Equal keys must land in the same bucket.
2. A key's hash and equality-relevant state must stay stable while it is in the table.

The reverse of rule 1 is *not* required: unequal keys may share a hash. That is just a collision.

In Python, immutable built-ins (`int`, `str`, `tuple` of hashables, `frozenset`) are hashable. The built-ins list, dict and set are not hashable. Mutability alone is not the general test: custom mutable objects can use stable identity equality/hashing, and an immutable class can disable hashing:

```python
d = {}
d[(1, 2)] = "ok"     # tuple: fine
d[[1, 2]] = "no"     # TypeError: unhashable
```

The second assignment deliberately fails: the tuple entry is stored, then the list key raises `TypeError` and execution stops unless the caller handles it.

> [!warning] Equal keys collapse
> Because `1 == 1.0 == True` in Python, they are the same dict key. `{1: "a", True: "b"}` gives `{1: "b"}`: the second assignment updates the value, keeping the first key object.

If you define `__eq__` on your own class, Python sets `__hash__` to `None`, making instances unhashable, unless you also define `__hash__`. In Java, overriding `equals` without `hashCode` is a classic bug: two equal objects can have different hashes, causing lookup to miss even if bucket reduction happens to coincide.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: filing by a name that can change
> An office files each customer's paperwork in a drawer chosen by the first letter of their surname. A customer marries and changes surname, but nobody moves the paperwork.
>
> **How it maps:** the surname is a key's equality-relevant state and the drawer is its bucket. Searching under the new name opens the wrong drawer; searching under the old name finds paperwork whose name no longer matches. The paperwork is still in the cabinet but unreachable, just like a mutated key in a set.
>
> **Where it stops:** a clerk could notice and refile the paperwork. A hash table never notices a mutation, so you must remove the key before changing it and reinsert it afterwards, or use a stable key such as a customer ID.

## Designing a key safely

Separate an object’s identity from its current contents. A mutable customer record can be stored as a value while its stable customer ID is the key. Updating the record’s address then leaves the index intact. Using all mutable fields as the key makes every change an index-maintenance operation instead.

For a custom value object, choose the same fields for equality and hashing. Two points considered equal by their coordinates must hash from those coordinates as well. If coordinates can change, freeze the key object or remove it before changing the fields and reinsert it afterwards. Defining a hash from one field and equality from another does not satisfy the contract.

A tuple is not automatically a safe key just because the outer container is immutable. Its elements must also be hashable; a tuple containing a list fails when hashed. A frozenset, unlike a set, is immutable and hashable. Neither object promises that a bad custom element implementation becomes sound merely by being wrapped.

## Key takeaways
- Equal keys must have equal hashes; unequal keys may collide.
- Hash and equality-relevant state must remain stable while a key is stored.
- Immutable containers require hashable elements; mutability alone is not the general test.

## Further reading
- [Python 3.14 data model: hashing](https://docs.python.org/3.14/reference/datamodel.html#object.__hash__)

options.text: `1 bool`
options.explanation: Correct. `1 == 1.0 == True` and their hashes match, so all three assignments hit the same entry. The last write wins, giving the value `"bool"`.

options.text: `TypeError`

options.explanation: Correct. A tuple of hashable items is hashable, because the tuple cannot change after creation.

options.explanation: Correct. Strings are immutable, so their hash never changes.
Lists are mutable. If a list key changed after insertion its hash would change and the entry would be lost, so lists are unhashable.

| `(1, 2)` | yes | yes |
| `"abc"` | yes | yes |
| `[1, 2]` | no | no |
| `frozenset` | yes | yes |
| `(1, [2])` | contains list | no |

For arbitrary classes, mutability alone does not determine hashability. Custom identity-based mutable objects can be hashable; keys must keep hash and equality behaviour stable.

options.text: `false`, because the two objects have different identity-based hash codes
options.explanation: The stated different hashes violate the equal-objects/equal-hashes contract, so the lookup returns false.

options.text: A compile error, because `hashCode` is required
options.explanation: Java compiles this fine; `Object` provides a default `hashCode`. The bug only shows up at run time, which is why it is so common.

options.text: `true`, because `HashSet` compares every element with `equals`

1. Java requires equal objects to have equal hash codes.
2. Object.hashCode does not guarantee distinct codes for distinct identities, so this question explicitly assumes different codes.

questions.prompt:
On CPython 3.14, what does this print? This deliberately violates the hash-key contract; do not rely on the outcome portably.

```python
# Changing equality state breaks lookup.
class P:
    def __init__(s, x): s.x = x
    def __eq__(s, o): return s.x == o.x
    def __hash__(s): return hash(s.x)

p = P(1)
s = {p}
p.x = 2
print(p in s, P(1) in s)
```

options.text: `True True`
options.explanation: This assumes the set tracks the object after mutation. The set stored `p` in the bucket for hash 1 and never moves it.

options.text: `True False`
options.explanation: `p in s` now hashes to `hash(2)` and looks in a different bucket from where `p` sits, so it does not find it.

options.text: `False True`
options.explanation: `P(1)` hashes to the right bucket and finds `p` there, but then compares with `==`: `p.x` is now 2, which is not equal to 1.

options.text: `False False`
options.explanation: Correct. The entry is stranded: its stored position matches hash 1, but its value now equals 2. Neither lookup can find it.

questions.workedExample:
1. `s = {p}` stores `p` at the slot chosen by `hash(1)`.
2. `p.x = 2` changes the object, but the set does not know.
3. `p in s`: computes `hash(2)`, looks in that slot, finds nothing: `False`.
4. `P(1) in s`: computes `hash(1)`, finds `p` in that slot, then checks `p == P(1)`, i.e. `2 == 1`: `False`.
5. Output: `False False`. The entry is still in the set (`len(s)` is 1) but unreachable by lookup. This is why keys must not change their hash while stored.

lessons.title: Lookup, deduplication and representation
lessons.summary: Once key equality is sound, choose a representation from the actual query.
lessons.body:
Once key equality is sound, choose a representation from the actual query. A prebuilt membership index can save repeated scans, while range queries and small dense integer domains often need a different structure.

## When to reach for a hash map or set

Most uses fall into three patterns.

### 1. Lookups by key

Replace a repeated linear search with one O(n) build (n being the number of items you index) and O(1) average lookups.

```python
# Partial example: supplied user objects.
# Build once, then probe for each order.
users = {u.id: u for u in user_list}
for order in orders:
    user = users.get(order.user_id)
```

For m orders and n users (here m counts orders, not buckets) this is O(n + m), instead of O(n × m) with a nested loop. With 10,000 users and 10,000 orders that is about 20,000 steps instead of 100 million.

### 2. Deduplication and "seen before?"

```python
def first_repeat(items):
    seen = set()
    for x in items:
        # Return the first value seen twice.
        if x in seen:
            return x
        seen.add(x)
    return None

first_repeat([3, 1, 4, 1, 5])  # 1
```

Checking `x in some_list` inside a loop is a common hidden O(n²): for n items, each of the n checks can scan up to n list entries. Changing the list to a set is often the single biggest speed-up available in a slow script.

### 3. Counting

```python
from collections import Counter

words = "the cat and the hat".split()
# Count token appearances, not positions.
counts = Counter(words)
counts["the"]          # 2
counts.most_common(1)  # [('the', 2)]
```

`Counter` is a dict subclass. The hand-written version is `counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1`. A related tool, `defaultdict(list)`, groups items by key without checking whether the key exists first.

## When not to use one

Hash tables are fast at exact-match lookups and nothing else. Reach for something different when:

- **You need order or ranges.** "All keys between 100 and 200", "the smallest key" or "the next key after x" need a sorted structure: a balanced binary search tree (Java's `TreeMap`, O(log n) per operation for n keys, about 20 steps for a million keys), a B-tree in a database, or a sorted array with binary search. A hash table would have to scan everything.
- **Keys are small dense integers.** If keys are 0 to 999, a plain array avoids hashing and often reduces overhead; actual performance depends on representation and workload.
- **Memory is tight.** Hash tables keep spare empty slots and per-entry overhead. For example, on a 64-bit CPython 3.14 build, sys.getsizeof(list(range(1_000_000))) is about 8 MB and sys.getsizeof(set(range(1_000_000))) about 33.6 MB, excluding integer objects. These sizes are build- and construction-dependent.
- **You need guaranteed worst-case latency.** A resize or a burst of collisions can make one operation take far longer than usual.

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Exact lookup, membership | Hash map / set |
| Sorted order, range query | Balanced BST, B-tree |
| Keys are 0..n | Plain array |
| Min or max repeatedly | Heap |

## Key takeaways
- Build a membership index once to avoid repeated list scans.
- Use sorted structures for ordered range queries and direct arrays for dense integer domains.
- Account for spare slots, representation overhead and latency spikes when choosing a table.

## Further reading
- [Time complexity of Python operations — Python wiki](https://wiki.python.org/moin/TimeComplexity)
- [collections: Counter and defaultdict — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html)

questions.prompt:
A nightly job checks incoming emails against a blocklist:

```python
# Supplied functions and email fixtures.
# Every membership test scans this list.
blocked = load_list()  # a list
for e in emails:
    if e in blocked:
        reject(e)
```

When both the email batch and the blocklist were 10,000 long, it took about a second. Both have now grown to 100,000 and the job takes nearly two minutes. What explains the slowdown, and what is the fix?

options.text: Ten times more data should mean ten times longer, so something else is wrong
options.explanation: This treats `in` on a list as O(1). A list membership test scans element by element, so the work grows with emails × blocklist size, not with either alone.

options.text: Each `in` scans the list, so work grows with emails × blocklist; build `set(blocked)` once and test against that
options.explanation: Correct. Ten times more emails, each scanning a ten-times-longer list, is about a hundred times the comparisons. A set built once makes each check expected O(1), so the job grows linearly again under ordinary hashing assumptions.

options.text: Sort the list, so `in` switches to binary search
options.explanation: List membership never switches to binary search, sorted or not. The bisect module can binary search a sorted list, but that is a different design with logarithmic lookups.

options.text: Nothing can be done: checking 100,000 emails against 100,000 addresses is inherently quadratic
options.explanation: Only the list representation makes it quadratic. A hash set answers each membership test in expected constant time, removing the multiplying factor.

questions.workedExample:
1. `e in blocked` on a list compares `e` with entries one at a time, up to the whole list.
2. So the job does (number of emails) × (blocklist length) comparisons in the worst case. Growing both by 10× multiplies that by about 100: one second becomes on the order of a hundred seconds, matching the symptom.
3. Fix: `blocked = set(load_list())` once, before the loop. Building the set is one pass over the blocklist, and each check is then an expected O(1) hash lookup.
4. Total expected work becomes proportional to emails + blocklist size. Actual time still depends on string hashing and equality, memory and caching, so measure the result rather than assuming an exact speed-up.

questions.prompt: You store 50 million orders keyed by timestamp. The main query is "all orders between 09:00 and 09:05". Which structure fits best?

options.text: A sorted structure such as a balanced BST or B-tree index on timestamp
options.explanation: Correct. Keys are kept in order, so with n stored orders you find 09:00 in O(log n) steps and walk forward until 09:05, costing O(log n + k) for k results.

options.text: A hash map from timestamp to order
options.explanation: A hash map only answers exact-match lookups. Hashing scatters neighbouring timestamps across the table, so a range query would have to scan every entry.

options.text: A hash set of timestamps
options.explanation: A set has the same problem as a map: no ordering, so no efficient range scan.

options.text: An unsorted array, scanned each time
options.explanation: That works but costs O(n) per query: 50 million checks to return a few thousand rows.

questions.workedExample:
1. Identify the query type: a **range** query, not an exact lookup.
2. A good hash function deliberately destroys ordering: `09:00:01` and `09:00:02` end up in unrelated buckets.
3. A sorted structure keeps neighbours together. Search for the first key ≥ 09:00, then iterate in order. The search is logarithmic. Each step halves the remaining range, so about 26 halvings narrow 50 million keys to one position (2²⁶ is about 67 million).

questions.prompt: You count events by error code. Codes are integers from 0 to 999, and you process 100 million events. Which representation uses direct addressing and avoids hashing these keys?

options.text: `collections.Counter()`
options.explanation: It works and is O(1) average per event, but each increment hashes the key and probes a table. With small dense integer keys, that work is unnecessary.

options.text: `counts = [0] * 1000` and `counts[code] += 1`
options.explanation: Correct. When keys are dense small integers, the key *is* the index. No hashing, no collisions, no resizing, and 1,000 slots use far less memory than a dict of 1,000 entries.

options.text: A sorted list with `bisect` to find each code
options.explanation: Binary search is unnecessary to locate a known dense index; actual speed of complete implementations still needs measurement.

options.text: A `set` of codes seen
options.explanation: A set records presence, not counts, so it cannot answer "how many".

questions.workedExample:
1. A hash table is a general way to map arbitrary keys to array slots.
2. Here the keys are already array indices: 0 to 999. This is called direct addressing.
3. `counts[code] += 1` reads and updates an indexed slot. A dict increment hashes the key, finds the slot, compares, and stores.
4. Both are O(1), but over 10⁸ events implementation constants matter and should be measured, and the array needs no per-entry overhead.
5. Rule of thumb: dense small integer keys → array; sparse or non-integer keys → hash map.

questions.prompt: A service holds `big`, a list of 10 million product IDs that rarely changes. Thousands of times a day it receives a list of about 10 IDs and must return those present in `big`. Assume enough memory for a set and bounded-cost well-distributed hashes. Which gives expected O(len(small)) per-request work while preserving small-list order and duplicates?

options.text: `set(big) & set(small)` for each request
options.explanation: This rebuilds the large set for each request and returns a set, losing input order and duplicate occurrences.

options.text: `[x for x in small if x in big]` for each request
options.explanation: No set at all: each `x in big` scans the list, so a request costs about 10 × 10⁷ = 10⁸ comparisons.

options.text: Build `big_set = set(big)` once at start-up, then `[x for x in small if x in big_set]` per request
options.explanation: Correct. Pay O(N) once, where N is the 10 million IDs in `big`, then each request costs about 10 O(1) lookups. This is the build-once, query-many pattern.

options.text: Sort `big` once, then binary search each ID
options.explanation: Sorting once gives logarithmic comparisons per lookup. It may offer memory or locality advantages, but not the requested expected constant lookup bound.

questions.workedExample: Build big_set once in expected O(N), where N is the length of `big`, then retain each small-list item if it belongs to that set. This preserves request order and duplicates with expected O(len(small)) table work. A sorted representation remains a valid trade-off; the asymptotic bound is not a wall-clock benchmark.

lessons.title: Hash quality and bucket reduction
lessons.summary: A full hash and a bucket index are different things; a power-of-two remainder exposes patterns in a key's low bits.
lessons.body:
A hash table is only as good as its hash function. Feed it keys that the function spreads evenly and every bucket holds about one key. Feed it keys that the function clumps together and the table turns into a slow list.

There are two steps to watch. The hash function turns a key into a large integer, and a second step reduces that integer to a bucket index. Even a valid hash can perform badly if the reduction preserves patterns in the input.

## What a table hash needs

A hash function maps a key of any size to a fixed-size integer. For a hash table it must be:

1. **Deterministic.** The same key always gives the same hash, at least within one run of the program.
2. **Consistent with equality.** If `a == b`, then `hash(a) == hash(b)`.
3. **Uniform.** Keys spread evenly over the output range, *including* the patterned keys real programs produce: sequential IDs, multiples of 1,000, strings sharing a long prefix.
4. **Fast.** It runs on every lookup, so a few nanoseconds matters.

A good hash also has the **avalanche** property: flipping one input bit flips about half the output bits. That stops similar keys (`user1`, `user2`) landing in nearby slots.

Table hashes are not cryptographic hashes. SHA-256 is designed to make finding two inputs with the same output computationally infeasible, and pays for that in speed. A table only needs a good spread, so it uses fast non-cryptographic functions such as MurmurHash, xxHash or wyhash, or a keyed function such as SipHash when attackers control the keys (Hash flooding and runtime randomisation).



## From hash to bucket: the division method

The simplest way to turn an integer key into one of m buckets is the **division method**: divide by m and keep the remainder (written `k mod m`, or `k % m` in Python). Key 40 in a 13-bucket table goes to bucket 1, because 40 = 3 × 13 + 1.

It is fast, but the choice of m matters enormously. Take keys that are all multiples of 8 (common for memory addresses and aligned sizes):

```
keys:      8  16  24  32  40  48  56  64
mod 16:    8   0   8   0   8   0   8   0
mod 13:    8   3  11   6   1   9   4  12
```

With sixteen buckets, the keys use only 2 of 16 buckets. With thirteen buckets, they spread over 8 different buckets.

Why? When m is a power of two (2, 4, 8, 16, …), the remainder is just the key's lowest binary digits: 40 is 101000 in binary, and its remainder after dividing by 16 is its last four bits, 1000, which is 8. Every multiple of 8 ends in three zero bits, so only one of the four kept bits can vary. Any pattern in the low bits goes straight into the bucket index. The textbook advice for the division method is to choose m as a **prime not close to a power of two**; the next lesson shows how other designs keep fast power-of-two sizes by mixing the bits first.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: filing by the last digit
> A clerk files invoices in ten trays by the last digit of the invoice number. That works well until the accounts system starts issuing numbers that always end in 0 or 5: two trays overflow and eight sit empty.
>
> **How it maps:** the trays are buckets, "last digit" is reduction by a power of the number base (keeping the low digits), and the 0-or-5 numbering is a pattern in the keys' low bits, like aligned memory addresses that always end in zero bits.
>
> **Where it stops:** the clerk works in decimal, so the low digits are the last decimal digits; a power-of-two table keeps the last binary digits. Choosing a prime number of trays, or scrambling the number before filing, spreads such patterned keys out.

## Key takeaways
- Hashing must respect equality and remain deterministic for the table’s lifetime.
- Power-of-two remainder selection exposes patterns in low bits.
- A cryptographic collision guarantee is different from useful bucket distribution.

## Further reading
- [Hash function — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_function)

options.text: Keys spread across all 16 buckets
options.explanation: That needs the low bits of the keys to vary freely. Because 16 is a power of two, `% 16` keeps only the low 4 bits, and multiples of 8 always end in three zero bits.

options.text: Only 2 buckets ever used, 0 and 8, each holding half the keys
options.explanation: Correct. Multiples of 8 end in binary `1000` or `0000`, so their remainders by 16 are only ever 8 or 0. Fourteen buckets stay empty however many keys you add.

options.text: About 4 buckets used
options.explanation: This guesses at partial spreading. Only one of the four kept bits can vary, so there are exactly two possible remainders.

options.text: Every key in bucket 0
options.explanation: Only multiples of 16 have remainder 0. The odd multiples of 8 (8, 24, 40, …) land in bucket 8.

questions.workedExample:
1. Remainders by 16 alternate:

```
k     8 16 24 32 40 48 56 64
k%16  8  0  8  0  8  0  8  0
```

2. Why: dividing by a power of two and keeping the remainder keeps only the key's lowest binary digits. For 16 that is the last 4 bits.
3. Every multiple of 8 ends in three zero bits, so of those 4 bits only the top one can vary: the remainder is 0 or 8.
4. The table therefore behaves like a 2-bucket table, with chains (or probe runs) eight times longer than an even spread would give.
5. A prime size such as 13 gives remainders 8, 3, 11, 6, 1, 9, 4, 12 for the same keys; mixing the bits before reducing has the same effect for power-of-two tables.

questions.prompt: Which properties must a hash function have to be used correctly in a hash table? Select all that apply.

options.text: The same key gives the same hash for the lifetime of the table
options.explanation: Correct. Lookups recompute the hash; if it changed, the table would search the wrong bucket.

options.text: Equal keys give equal hashes
options.explanation: Correct. Otherwise two equal keys could sit in different buckets and lookups would miss.

options.text: Different keys give different hashes
options.explanation: Impossible in general (infinitely many keys, finitely many hashes) and not required: collisions are expected and handled.

options.text: It is infeasible to find two keys with the same hash
options.explanation: That is collision resistance, a cryptographic property. Tables work fine without it; they only need a good spread on ordinary input (and a keyed hash if inputs are hostile).

options.text: It produces the same values across machines and program runs
options.explanation: Not needed for an in-memory table, and Python deliberately avoids it by randomising string hashes per process.

questions.workedExample:
Separate what is needed for *correctness* from what is nice for *performance* or security:

1. **Deterministic within the table's lifetime.** Required for correctness.
2. **Consistent with equality.** Required for correctness.
3. **Injective.** Impossible and unnecessary: collision resolution exists for this.
4. **Collision resistant.** A cryptographic goal; it costs speed. For hostile input, a keyed hash such as SipHash is the practical answer.
5. **Stable across runs.** Only matters if you persist hashes, which you should not do with a table hash.

A function satisfying only the first two is *correct* but may still be slow (e.g. `return 0`). Uniformity is what makes it fast.

questions.prompt: A memory allocator tracks objects in a table of 1,024 buckets using `index = addr & 1023` (the low 10 bits of the address). Every address is a multiple of 16. Profiling shows lookups far slower than expected for the table's load factor. What will a bucket-occupancy dump show, and why?

options.text: All 1,024 buckets evenly used; the slowdown must come from elsewhere
options.explanation: This assumes the low bits are random. Because every address is a multiple of 16, the lowest 4 bits are always zero, so many buckets can never be chosen.

options.text: Only buckets 0 to 15 used, because the alignment is 16
options.explanation: This reads the alignment as the number of usable buckets. The fixed bits are the lowest ones, so the usable indices are spaced 16 apart across the whole range, not packed at the start.

options.text: Only 16 buckets are missing; the rest are fine
options.explanation: Alignment does not remove a handful of buckets. It removes every index that is not a multiple of 16.

options.text: Only every 16th bucket (0, 16, 32, …, 1008) is used: 64 buckets, each with about 16 times its fair share of entries
options.explanation: Correct. Bits 0 to 3 are always zero, so only bits 4 to 9 vary: 2⁶ = 64 reachable indices. The effective load is 16 times higher than the nominal load factor suggests.

questions.workedExample:
1. `addr & 1023` keeps bits 0 to 9 of the address (`&` is bitwise AND; 1023 is ten 1-bits).
2. A multiple of 16 always has bits 0 to 3 equal to zero, so every index is itself a multiple of 16: 0, 16, 32, …, 1008.
3. Only the 6 bits from bit 4 to bit 9 vary, so 2⁶ = 64 of the 1,024 buckets are reachable. Each holds about 16 times as many entries as an even spread would give: that is the slowdown.
4. Fixes: shift off the known-zero bits first, or multiply by a large odd constant and take the *high* bits (Fibonacci hashing), or use mixing suited to the actual address patterns. Java's `h ^ (h >>> 16)` helps only when varying high bits fold into the selected low bits; for addresses below 65,536 the shifted term is zero.

lessons.title: Multiplication and Fibonacci hashing
lessons.summary: Multiplying by a golden-ratio constant and keeping the high bits lets a power-of-two table spread patterned keys.
lessons.body:
Prime table sizes fix the low-bit problem but are awkward: the table cannot double neatly, and reducing by a variable prime needs a division. Multiplication hashing lets the table size stay a power of two by mixing the key's bits *before* choosing a bucket.

## The multiplication method

Multiply the key by a constant between 0 and 1, keep only the part after the decimal point, and scale that fraction up to the table size. Knuth suggests the constant 0.618…, the fractional part of the golden ratio. For key 8 and 16 buckets: 8 × 0.618034 ≈ 4.944, the fractional part is 0.944, and 16 × 0.944 ≈ 15.1, so the key goes to bucket 15.

The multiplication scrambles every key's fraction, so neighbouring or aligned keys end up far apart and the table size no longer has to be prime. The method assumes integer keys; strings and tuples are first turned into integers.

In integer arithmetic this becomes **Fibonacci hashing**: multiply by a large odd constant, let the product overflow to 32 bits, and use the *top* p bits of the result as the bucket index (4 bits for a 16-bucket table). The top bits are the ones every bit of the key has influenced, which is exactly what the low-bit remainder lacked.

```formula reference
h(k) = floor(((kA) mod 2^32) / 2^(32 − p))
where
h(k): the bucket index for key k, from 0 to 2^p − 1
k: the non-negative integer key
A: the constant 2,654,435,769, which is 2^32 divided by the golden ratio (about 1.618), rounded to an odd number
p: the number of index bits, so the table has 2^p buckets
mod: "modulo", the remainder after division; mod 2^32 keeps the low 32 bits, as a 32-bit unsigned multiply does automatically
floor: round down to a whole number; dividing by 2^(32 − p) and rounding down keeps the top p of the 32 bits
^: "to the power of"
In words: multiply the key by a fixed odd constant, keep 32 bits of the product, and use their highest bits as the bucket number. This is the integer version of "keep the fraction and scale it up".
```

The same calculation in Python, where `%` is mod and `>>` shifts bits right (dividing by a power of two and rounding down):

```python
def fib_hash(k, p):
    if not 0 <= p <= 32:
        raise ValueError("p out of range")
    # 2**32 / golden ratio
    A = 2654435769
    # Keep 32 bits, then take high index
    # bits.
    return ((k * A) % 2**32) >> (32 - p)
```

For a table of 2⁴ = 16 buckets, the aligned keys 8, 16, 24, …, 64, which shared just two buckets under `k % 16`, map to 15, 14, 13, 12, 11, 10, 9 and 8: all different. This fixed 32-bit mapping improves this example; it is not a universal collision or avalanche guarantee. Inputs differing by 2³² (about 4.3 billion) collide because the product is reduced modulo 2³².

## Key takeaways
- Multiplication uses a fractional product to choose a bucket.
- The fixed-width version keeps a word-sized product then extracts high index bits.
- The worked alignment example does not guarantee good distribution for every key set.

## Further reading
- [Hash function — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_function)

questions.prompt:
A 16-bucket table stores keys that are all multiples of 8. Version A picks buckets with `k % 16`. Version B uses Fibonacci hashing:

```python

A = 2654435769
b = ((k * A) % 2**32) >> 28
```

Why does version B spread these keys better?

options.text: The multiply lets every bit of the key influence the top bits, and B keeps the top bits rather than the low ones
options.explanation: Correct. In A the bucket is the key's own low 4 bits, which alignment pins to 0 or 8. In B the product's high bits depend on all of the key's bits, so keys 8, 16, …, 64 land in eight different buckets (15 down to 8).

options.text: B uses a prime table size
options.explanation: Both versions use 16 buckets, a power of two. Avoiding a prime size is the point of the multiplication method.

options.text: B guarantees that no two distinct keys ever share a bucket
options.explanation: No 16-bucket scheme can do that for more than 16 keys. B also maps keys that differ by exactly 2³² to the same bucket, because the product is cut to 32 bits.

options.text: The constant A is random, so B behaves like universal hashing
options.explanation: A is a fixed public constant, not a randomly chosen function, so B gives no protection against adversarial keys.

questions.workedExample:
1. Version A keeps the key's lowest 4 bits. Every multiple of 8 ends in three zero bits, so only buckets 0 and 8 are possible.
2. Version B multiplies first. Each bit of the key is added into many higher bits of the product, so the product's top bits depend on the whole key.
3. Shifting right by 28 keeps the top 4 of the 32 bits. Running it for 8, 16, 24, …, 64 gives buckets 15, 14, 13, 12, 11, 10, 9 and 8: eight different buckets instead of two.
4. Limits: this is one good example, not a guarantee for every key set, and a fixed public constant gives no defence against an attacker choosing keys.

lessons.title: Polynomial hashes and character order
lessons.summary: Weighting each character by its position stops anagrams colliding systematically, and Horner's rule computes it in one pass.
lessons.body:
A string hash must use the *order* of the characters, not just which characters appear. Otherwise every rearrangement of the same letters collides.

## Hashing strings: polynomial hashes

A string is a sequence of characters, and each character has a numeric code (`a` is 97 in ASCII and Unicode). A naive hash adds the character codes, but then every anagram collides: `"listen"` and `"silent"` both sum to 655.

A **polynomial hash** fixes this by giving each position a different weight: the last character is multiplied by 1, the one before it by a base p (such as 31), the one before that by p², and so on. The weighted sum is reduced modulo a large number M to keep it a manageable size. Order now matters: with base 31, `"abc"` hashes to 96,354 but `"cab"` to 98,244, because whichever character comes first carries the biggest weight.

```formula reference
h(s) = (c_0 p^(n − 1) + c_1 p^(n − 2)
        + … + c_(n−1)) mod M
where
h(s): the hash of string s, a whole number from 0 to M − 1
s: the string being hashed
n: the number of characters in s
c_0: the numeric code of the first character
c_1: the numeric code of the second character
c_(n−1): the code of the last character, which gets weight 1
p: the base, a fixed whole number such as 31
M: the modulus, a large number such as the prime 1,000,000,009
mod: "modulo", the remainder after dividing by M
…: the terms in between follow the same pattern
^: "to the power of"
In words: multiply each character's code by the base raised to a power that falls by one per position, add the results and keep the remainder after dividing by M.
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: place value in ordinary numbers
> The digits 1, 2 and 3 can make 123 or 321. Same digits, different numbers, because the leftmost digit is worth hundreds and the rightmost only units.
>
> **How it maps:** a polynomial hash treats each character code as a "digit" in base p instead of base 10. The first character gets the highest power of the base, so rearranging the characters changes the total.
>
> **Where it stops:** decimal digits are always smaller than 10, so every digit string has exactly one value. Character codes are larger than a base such as 31, so different strings can add up to the same total, and the final remainder squeezes all strings into M values.

Position weights distinguish many rearrangements, but not all of them. A remainder has only finitely many values, and even before reduction two anagrams can share a weighted sum: with base 31, `"BAa"` and `"AaB"` both hash to 65,538. A matching hash is therefore only a candidate; the table still compares the actual strings.

You never compute the powers separately. **Horner's rule** walks the string once, multiplying the running total by the base and adding the next code, which gives every earlier character one more factor of the base:

```python
def poly_hash(s, p=31, M=10**9 + 9):
    h = 0
    for ch in s:
        # Shift old weights, add the new
        # code.
        h = (h * p + ord(ch)) % M
    return h

poly_hash("abc")
# 97*31^2 + 98*31 + 99 = 96354
```

Java's `String.hashCode` uses base 31 over UTF-16 code units, with signed 32-bit overflow instead of a prime modulus. Python's `ord` gives Unicode code points, so the code above differs from Java for supplementary characters (such as emoji) even with a modulus of 2³².

## Key takeaways
- Position-dependent weights avoid systematic anagram collisions.
- Horner’s rule accumulates a weighted hash in one pass.
- Python code points and Java UTF-16 code units differ for supplementary characters.

## Further reading
- [String hashing — cp-algorithms](https://cp-algorithms.com/string/string-hashing.html)

3. In `"abc"` the heavy position holds `a` (97); in `"cab"` it holds `c` (99). That position dominates, so `"cab"` hashes higher: 98,244 against 96,354.

5. Position weighting separates these anagrams, but it does not guarantee distinct hashes for every rearrangement: `"BAa"` and `"AaB"` share a hash with base 31.

lessons.title: Rolling string hashes and collision risk
lessons.summary: A rolling hash updates a sliding window in constant time, and the birthday paradox makes collisions appear far sooner than the hash range suggests.
lessons.body:
A rolling hash slides a fixed-length window along a string and updates the window's hash in a few arithmetic steps, instead of rehashing every character. That makes hash-based substring search fast, but it also raises a question this lesson answers: how soon do different strings start sharing a hash?

## Rolling a fixed-length window

Think of decimal digits first. Slide a three-digit window along 12345: going from 123 to 234, you remove the leading 1 (worth 100), shift what is left up one place (23 becomes 230) and add the new digit 4. You never re-read the 2 or the 3.

A polynomial hash rolls the same way, in base p instead of base 10. Remove the outgoing character's contribution, multiply by the base to shift every remaining character up one power, and add the incoming character with weight 1:

```formula essential
h_new = (h_old − c_out p^(n − 1)) × p + c_in
where
h_new: the hash of the window after sliding one place right
h_old: the hash of the window before sliding
c_out: the code of the character leaving on the left
c_in: the code of the character entering on the right
p: the base, such as 31
n: the window length in characters; p^(n − 1) is the weight the leaving character carried
^: "to the power of"
In words: subtract the leaving character's weighted contribution, shift everything up one power of the base, then add the arriving character. With base 31, "abc" (hash 96,354) rolls to "bcd" (hash 97,347).
```

With a modulus M, every step is also reduced mod M (adding M first if the subtraction went negative). With fixed-width arithmetic and the outgoing weight p^(n − 1) computed once in advance, each slide costs O(1), however long the window. That is the idea behind the Rabin–Karp substring search, which compares a pattern's hash with every window of a text in expected linear time and checks the real characters only when hashes match.

## How soon do collisions appear?

> [!warning] Small moduli collide sooner than you think
> With a modulus around 10⁹, 100,000 distinct strings almost certainly contain a pair with the same hash (about a 99% chance). If you compare strings by hash alone, use a 64-bit modulus or two independent hashes, and confirm matches with a real comparison.

The reason is the **birthday paradox**: what matters is the number of *pairs* of strings, which grows with the square of the number of strings. Collisions therefore appear long before the hash values run out: the chance of at least one shared hash reaches about 50% at only about 1.18 times the square root of the number of possible hashes (around 37,000 strings for a 10⁹-sized modulus).

```formula reference
P ≈ 1 − e^(−n^2 / (2M))
where
P: the probability that at least two of the strings share a hash, from 0 (never) to 1 (certain)
n: the number of distinct strings hashed
M: the number of possible hash values (the modulus)
e: Euler's number, about 2.718
^: "to the power of"
≈: approximately equal to; the approximation is good when n is much smaller than M
In words: the collision chance depends on the square of the number of strings compared with the size of the hash space, so it rises steeply long before the number of strings gets anywhere near the number of possible hashes.
```

This treats each string's hash as an independent, uniformly random value. Real hashes are not perfectly random, and patterned or deliberately chosen inputs can do worse.

## Key takeaways
- A rolling update removes the outgoing weight, shifts remaining weights and adds the incoming code.
- Constant update cost assumes fixed-width arithmetic and a precomputed outgoing weight.
- Collision risk grows with the number of pairs; confirm matching hashes with real comparisons.

## Further reading
- [String hashing — cp-algorithms](https://cp-algorithms.com/string/string-hashing.html)

A colleague argues: "There are only a million documents and over four billion possible hashes, so false merges can't happen." Assuming distinct documents with independent, uniformly distributed hashes, what should you expect?

options.text: Around a hundred pairs of different documents wrongly merged, because collisions grow with the number of pairs
options.explanation: Correct. A million documents form about 500 billion pairs, and each pair matches with probability 1 in 2³² (about 4.3 billion): roughly 116 colliding pairs expected.

options.text: Essentially none: a million is tiny compared with four billion
options.explanation: This is the birthday-paradox trap. The comparison that matters is pairs (about a million squared over two) against the hash space, not documents against the hash space.

options.text: About half the documents merged
options.explanation: That would need a hash space comparable to the number of documents. With 2³² possible values the expected number of colliding pairs is in the low hundreds.

options.text: It cannot be estimated without knowing the documents' contents
options.explanation: Under the stated uniform-hash assumption the contents do not matter; only the number of documents and the hash width do. Real hashes on patterned data can do worse, which is a reason to compare contents anyway.

questions.workedExample:
1. Count pairs, not documents: n documents form about n²/2 pairs. For a million that is about 5 × 10¹¹ pairs.
2. Each pair shares a 32-bit hash with probability 1 in 2³², about 1 in 4.3 billion.
3. Expected colliding pairs ≈ 5 × 10¹¹ ÷ 4.3 × 10⁹ ≈ 116: some false merges are almost certain.
4. Fixes: use a 64-bit or 128-bit hash (with 64 bits the expectation drops to about 3 × 10⁻⁸ pairs), or treat a hash match as a candidate and confirm with a full content comparison.

questions.prompt: A rolling polynomial hash over windows of 3 characters uses base 31 and, for simplicity, no modulus: the first character is weighted by 31² = 961, the second by 31 and the third by 1. The hash of `abc` is 96,354. Which expression gives `h("bcd")` from it in O(1)? (`a` has code 97; `d` has code 100.)

options.explanation: This treats the hash as a plain sum. The outgoing `a` was weighted by 31², so subtracting 97 removes far too little.
This shifts first, which also multiplies `a`'s contribution to 97 × 31³, then subtracts only 97. The outgoing term is not removed.

Correct. Remove the outgoing character's contribution (97 × 961), shift every remaining character up one power by multiplying by 31, then add the new character with weight 1. Result: 97,347, the same as hashing `bcd` from scratch.

This rolls the wrong way: it gives the arriving character the heaviest weight (31²), but a character entering on the right takes the lowest weight, 1. It also subtracts only 97 instead of a's weighted contribution (97 × 961).

questions.workedExample:
1. Compare the two windows' weights:

```
abc: a×961 + b×31 + c×1
bcd: b×961 + c×31 + d×1
```

2. Sliding drops `a`'s term and moves `b` and `c` up one power. So: subtract `a`'s term (97 × 961), multiply what is left by 31, then add `d`'s code with weight 1.
3. That is `(96354 - 97*31**2) * 31 + 100`, which gives 97,347; hashing `bcd` directly gives the same value.
4. The other options either forget the outgoing weight (subtracting just 97), shift before removing (so `a`'s term grows instead of disappearing), or put the new character in the heaviest position.

Each slide costs O(1), which is how Rabin–Karp compares a pattern with every window of a text of length n in O(n) expected time.

lessons.title: Universal hashing and adversary assumptions
lessons.summary: Picking the hash function at random bounds collisions for any keys chosen independently of that choice, but not for an attacker who adapts to it.
lessons.body:
Any *fixed* hash function has bad inputs. Universal hashing answers this by choosing the function at random when the table is created, so no particular set of keys is bad in advance.

## Universal hashing

There are infinitely many possible keys and only m buckets (m being the table size), so infinitely many keys share some bucket under any fixed function. That proves colliding inputs exist; it does not prove they are easy to find.

**Universal hashing** picks the function at random from a family (a large set of possible hash functions) when the table is created. A family is universal if, for any two distinct keys you name in advance, a randomly chosen member puts them in the same bucket no more often than a truly random bucket choice would:

```formula essential
Pr[h(x) = h(y)] ≤ 1 / m
where
Pr[…]: "the probability that …", a number from 0 (never) to 1 (always)
h: the hash function, picked at random from the family when the table is created
x: one key
y: a second key, different from x
m: the number of buckets
≤: "is at most"
In words: whichever two different keys you name in advance, the randomly chosen function puts them in the same bucket with probability at most 1 in m. With 1,000 buckets, that is at most 0.1%.
```

The probability is over the random choice of h, not over the keys. That is the whole point: even a fixed, worst-case set of keys gets short chains on average, provided the keys were chosen without knowing which function was picked and the load factor stays bounded.

The classic Carter–Wegman family for integer keys picks two random numbers when the table is created: multiply the key by the first, add the second, take the remainder by a fixed prime larger than any key, then the remainder by the table size. Each pair of random numbers is a different member of the family.

```formula reference
h(k) = ((ak + b) mod p) mod m
where
h(k): the bucket index for key k, from 0 to m − 1
k: a non-negative integer key smaller than p
a: a multiplier picked at random from 1 to p − 1 when the table is created
b: an offset picked at random from 0 to p − 1
p: a fixed prime number larger than every possible key
m: the number of buckets
mod: "modulo", the remainder after whole-number division
In words: multiply by a random number, add another random number, take the remainder by a prime, then by the table size. Changing the two random numbers gives a different function from the same family.
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a seating plan drawn after the guest list
> A wedding organiser fixes the guest list first, then draws table numbers at random. However awkward the guest list, it is unlikely that any two particular guests end up at the same table more often than chance.
>
> **How it maps:** the guests are the keys, chosen before the draw; the random draw is picking h from the family; "two particular guests at the same table" is the pairwise collision bound.
>
> **Where it stops:** if a guest could see the seating plan and then invite friends to fill their own table, chance no longer applies. That is an attacker who adapts to the outcome, and the universal-hashing guarantee does not cover it.

The guarantee covers a fixed key set chosen before the random function, including a hostile one. An attacker who can watch the table's behaviour and choose later keys accordingly needs a separate analysis; keeping a and b secret is not, on its own, that proof.

## Key takeaways
- The probability is over the random function choice, not the keys.
- Pairwise collision bounds apply to distinct keys chosen independently of the function.
- An attacker who chooses keys after seeing the table's behaviour needs a separate analysis.

## Further reading
- [Universal hashing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_hashing)

questions.prompt: A universal hash family guarantees that, for any two distinct keys x and y, the chance that h puts them in the same bucket is at most 1 in m, where m is the number of buckets. What is that probability taken over?

options.text: The random choice of keys x and y from all possible inputs
options.explanation: The pair is fixed independently of the function choice; the probability is over the sampled hash function.

options.text: The random choice of the function h from the family, made when the table is created
options.explanation: Correct. For each fixed distinct pair, sample the hash function from the universal family; collision probability is at most one divided by the bucket count.

options.text: The order in which keys are inserted
options.explanation: Insertion order affects which key ends up where in a chain or probe sequence, but not whether two keys hash to the same bucket.

options.text: The size of the table m, chosen at random
options.explanation: m is fixed by the table; the bound is stated in terms of it. The randomness is in the parameters of h, such as a and b.

questions.workedExample: Fix two distinct keys before sampling the hash function. The universal-family inequality bounds the probability over h. It supports expected chain bounds for a key set independent of the random choice. Attackers who choose keys after observing the table require additional analysis; secrecy of parameters alone does not establish the theorem for adaptively chosen keys.

lessons.title: Hash flooding and runtime randomisation
lessons.summary: When a client chooses keys, collisions become a security and latency concern.
lessons.body:
When an untrusted client chooses the keys, collisions stop being bad luck and become an attack. This lesson shows how such attacks work and how language runtimes defend against them.

## Hash flooding attacks

In 2003, Crosby and Wallach showed that you could slow a server to a crawl by sending keys that all collide in its hash table: an **algorithmic complexity attack**. Inserting n colliding keys costs O(n²), because each new key is compared with every key already in its chain: 50,000 colliding keys need about 1.25 billion comparisons.

In December 2011, at the 28C3 conference, Alexander Klink and Julian Wälde showed it working against PHP, Java, Python, Ruby and ASP.NET web stacks. Web frameworks parse POST parameters into a hash table automatically, so a single request could carry tens of thousands of colliding parameter names.

Java's string hash made colliding keys trivial to generate:

```
"Aa".hashCode() == 2112
"BB".hashCode() == 2112
```

Any string built from these two blocks collides with every other one of the same length: `"AaAa"`, `"AaBB"`, `"BBAa"` and `"BBBB"` all hash to 2,031,744. Thirty blocks gives 2³⁰ (about a billion) colliding keys.

Languages responded in several ways:

| Defence | Example |
|---|---|
| Random seed per process | Python 3.3+, Ruby, Perl |
| Keyed hash function | SipHash: Python, Rust |
| Cap request parameters | PHP `max_input_vars` |
| Tree-shaped buckets | Java 8 `HashMap` |

**SipHash** (Aumasson and Bernstein, 2012) is a fast keyed function designed for exactly this job: it mixes a secret 128-bit key into every hash, so without that key an attacker should not be able to predict which inputs collide. Python switched to it for `str` and `bytes` in 3.4 (PEP 456, using SipHash-2-4), and from 3.11 common CPython builds default to the slightly faster SipHash-1-3; `sys.hash_info.algorithm` shows what your build uses. Rust's standard `HashMap` currently defaults to SipHash-1-3 too, though its documentation says that may change.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a sorting office with a public rule
> A sorting office puts each parcel in a bin chosen by a published rule based on the address. A prankster who knows the rule can address ten thousand parcels so they all land in one bin, and that bin's clerk grinds to a halt. If the office changes to a secret rule each morning, the prankster can no longer aim.
>
> **How it maps:** the published rule is a fixed public hash such as Java's `String.hashCode`, the overloaded bin is one long chain, and the secret daily rule is a keyed hash like SipHash with a per-process random key.
>
> **Where it stops:** the secret only helps while it stays secret and the function resists analysis. It does nothing about a prankster who simply sends a huge number of parcels, so size limits are still needed, and some keys (such as Python integers) are not randomised at all.

> [!note] Consequences of randomisation
> In Python, `hash("abc")` differs between runs unless you set the `PYTHONHASHSEED` environment variable. Never store `hash()` results in files or send them between processes.

Integers are not randomised. On common 64-bit CPython builds, a non-negative integer hashes to its remainder after dividing by the prime 2⁶¹ − 1 (`sys.hash_info.modulus`), and a negative integer to minus the hash of its magnitude. So small integers hash to themselves, and 2⁶¹ hashes to 1. One special case: CPython never returns −1 as a hash, because −1 signals an error inside the interpreter, so `hash(-1) == -2` and `hash(-1) == hash(-2)`. Hash randomisation therefore does nothing for integer keys an attacker controls; other defences, such as limits on input size, still matter.

## Key takeaways
- Public deterministic hashes can let attackers construct expensive collision chains.
- Keyed hashing and per-process randomisation make predicting collisions harder.
- Python integer hashes remain deterministic, and built-in hash results are unsuitable for persisted placement.

## Further reading
- [Denial of Service via Algorithmic Complexity Attacks (Crosby and Wallach, USENIX Security 2003)](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/sec03/tech/full_papers/crosby/crosby.pdf)
- [PEP 456: Secure and interchangeable hash algorithm](https://peps.python.org/pep-0456/)

questions.prompt: You run `python3 -c 'print(hash("abc"))'` twice and get two different numbers. Why?

options.text: Python's string hash is randomised per process with a secret seed, to defend against hash flooding
options.explanation: Per-process randomisation makes reusable precomputed attacks harder; PYTHONHASHSEED can override it.

options.text: `hash()` includes the object's memory address
options.explanation: String hashes use contents and a process secret. Default object hashing is identity-based; an address relationship is an implementation detail.

options.text: It is a bug: hash functions must be deterministic
options.explanation: They must be deterministic *within one process*, which this is. Across processes, Python deliberately varies them.

options.text: Strings are hashed with SHA-256, which includes a random nonce
options.explanation: Common recent CPython builds use SipHash-1-3 for strings, configurable by the build; SHA-256 itself has no random nonce.

questions.workedExample:
1. A stored key needs a stable hash while its table uses it.
2. CPython normally chooses a process hash secret at startup; string hashes can consequently differ across runs.
3. This impedes reusable collision attacks but is not a proof that all adversarial inputs are harmless.
4. Do not persist Python hash values as stable identifiers; use an explicitly chosen stable digest when needed.

questions.prompt: Java's String.hashCode multiplies the running hash by thirty-one and adds each next UTF-16 code unit, with signed thirty-two-bit overflow. `"AaBB".hashCode()` is 2,031,744. Which of these have the same hash code? Select all that apply. (`A`=65, `B`=66, `a`=97, `C`=67, `#`=35)

options.text: `"AaAa"`
options.explanation: Correct. `Aa` and `BB` both hash to 2112 as two-character blocks, so any 4-character string built from those blocks gives 2112 × 31² + 2112.

options.text: `"BBBB"`
options.explanation: Correct. Same reason: two blocks each hashing to 2112.

options.text: `"ABBa"`
options.explanation: This mixes the letters across block boundaries: `AB` hashes to 65 × 31 + 66 = 2081, not 2112, so the total differs (2,001,984).
Correct. `C#` is 67 × 31 + 35 = 2077 + 35 = 2112, another block equivalent to `Aa`.

options.text: `"aABB"`
options.explanation: Swapping the case moves weight between positions: `aA` is 97 × 31 + 65 = 3072, not 2112.

questions.workedExample:
1. Java's string hash multiplies the running total by 31 and adds the next character. For a 4-character string, that means: hash of the first pair × 31², plus hash of the second pair. So two 4-character strings collide whenever their pairs have equal pair hashes.
2. Pair hashes (first code × 31, plus second code):

```
Aa: 65×31 + 97 = 2112
BB: 66×31 + 66 = 2112
C#: 67×31 + 35 = 2112
AB: 65×31 + 66 = 2081
aA: 97×31 + 65 = 3072
```

3. `AaAa`, `BBBB` and `C#BB` are built only from 2112-pairs, so they all hash to 2112 × 961 + 2112 = 2,031,744, the same as `AaBB`. `ABBa` splits into `AB` and `Ba`, and `aABB` starts with `aA`: both differ.
4. Each extra pair position doubles the number of colliding strings (or triples it when `C#` is also allowed). That cheap supply of collisions was the raw material of the 2011 flooding attacks.

questions.prompt: An API server parses JSON request bodies into a hash table using a fixed, public, unkeyed string hash with chaining. An attacker sends one 2 MB body containing 50,000 distinct keys that all have identical full hash values. Which best describes the cost and the appropriate primary defence among these choices?

options.text: Linear cost, about one comparison per key; reject bodies over 1 MB
options.explanation: Linear cost is what you get with no collisions. Colliding keys make each insert scan the existing chain. A size limit helps, but a few thousand colliding keys still fit in a small body.

options.text: Quadratic cost, over a billion comparisons for this one request; switch to a keyed hash with a secret random seed, such as SipHash
options.explanation: Correct. Each insert compares the new key with every key already in the chain, roughly half of 50,000² in total: about 1.25 billion comparisons. A secret keyed hash stops attackers predicting collisions; bound parsing resources as well.

options.text: Quadratic cost; use SHA-256 as the table hash
options.explanation: An unkeyed hash, even SHA-256, is public: the attacker only needs keys that share a *bucket*, which depends on a few bits of the hash and can be brute-forced offline. It is also much slower than a table hash.

options.text: Quadratic cost; increase the table's initial size
options.explanation: A larger table does not help: the keys collide on the full hash value, so they share a bucket at any table size.

questions.workedExample:
1. Every key lands in the same chain, and each insert compares the new key with every key already there to rule out a duplicate. The k-th key costs about k comparisons, so the total is about half of n² for n keys.
2. For 50,000 keys that is about 1.25 billion comparisons from a single 2 MB request, which is why one request can tie up a server.
3. Equal full hashes remain equal after any bucket reduction, so enlarging the table does not separate them.
4. Use a keyed, randomised hash, explicit JSON member and body limits, and resource budgets. Java tree bins give logarithmic lookup when hashes or a consistent comparable order distinguish keys. PHP's `max_input_vars` limits input parameters, not arbitrary decoded JSON members.

questions.prompt: A team sets `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` in its production containers so that log output involving sets is identical across restarts. The service accepts arbitrary JSON from the internet. What is the main risk?

options.text: None: Python 3.4+ uses SipHash, which is immune to collisions
options.explanation: No finite hash is collision-free. A fixed known seed removes process-secret randomisation, though this alone does not establish a practical collision attack.

options.text: String hashes become reproducible, removing per-process randomisation as a defence
options.explanation: This permits environment-specific precomputation. Practical attack cost still depends on hash width and the actual table probe algorithm.

options.text: Integer keys become randomised and break the service
options.explanation: The opposite: the setting turns randomisation *off*, and integer hashes are never randomised anyway.

options.text: Dict iteration order becomes random
options.explanation: Dict order is insertion order regardless of the seed. The seed only affects hash values (and so set iteration order).

questions.workedExample:
1. `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` disables string-hash randomisation.
2. A known seed does not by itself make large sets of full 64-bit SipHash collisions easy to find.
3. Sharing an initial bucket alone also does not prove quadratic CPython insertion: its perturbation sequence uses higher hash bits.
4. Retain randomisation for untrusted input, and sort supported values explicitly for deterministic logs. Fixed seeds do not make set order a language guarantee.
