lessons.title: Hash placement when server counts change
lessons.summary: Placing keys on servers by remainder moves most keys when a server is added; consistent hashing moves only the new server's share.
lessons.body:
Bucket reduction has a second life outside a single table: choosing which server stores a key. Here the problem is not a bad collision rate. Changing the divisor can move almost every key even when the hash itself is excellent.

## Hashing in distributed systems

A sharded cache or database must decide which server owns each key. The naive rule takes the key's stable full hash, divides by the number of servers N, and uses the remainder as the server number. It works until N changes, because then the remainder changes for most keys:

```formula reference
F ≈ N / (N + 1)
where
F: the fraction of keys that move to a different server when one server is added, from 0 to 1
N: the number of servers before the change
≈: approximately equal to; assumes uniformly spread hashes
In words: adding one server to N moves nearly every key, about N out of every N + 1.
```

Going from 10 to 11 servers moves about 10 keys in every 11, roughly 91% of the data, even though only one server was added. Doubling the server count moves about half. Either way a large share of a cache is invalidated at once, which is why distributed systems use **consistent hashing**: ideally only the new server's share moves, about 1 key in 11 (9%) for the same change. Consistent hashing is covered in the System Design subject.

## Why the remapping matters

Consider cached customer profiles spread across ten servers. When an eleventh server is added, recomputing the remainder sends most requests to a different server, even though each profile's hash and contents never changed. The old copy may still sit on its former server, but the new rule will not look there. A cache must refill or migrate those entries; a database must coordinate movement and ownership more carefully.

Consistent hashing instead places servers and keys on a ring, and each key belongs to the next server round the ring. Adding a server changes only the stretch of the ring it takes over. The ideal movement of only the new server's share assumes balanced ownership and uniformly distributed keys; finite rings, skewed workloads and replication change how much data or traffic actually moves.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: assigning parcels to delivery vans
> A depot assigns each street to a van by taking the street's number and dividing by the number of vans, using the remainder. When a new van joins, almost every street gets a different van, and every driver's local knowledge is wasted at once.
>
> **How it maps:** streets are keys, vans are servers and the remainder rule is mod-N placement. Consistent hashing is like giving each van a stretch of the ring road: a new van takes over part of one neighbour's stretch, and every other route is unchanged.
>
> **Where it stops:** a depot can reassign routes over a week; a cache sees the change instantly, as misses for every moved key. Real consistent-hashing rings also need many virtual positions per server to keep the stretches balanced.

Do not confuse remapping with hash randomisation. A per-process string hash such as Python's built-in `hash()` is unsuitable for placement: every client and server must compute the same stable hash with the same placement configuration. A stable placement hash can still need a separate defence if untrusted clients deliberately send traffic to hot keys.

## Key takeaways
- Changing the server-count divisor can remap most keys.
- Ideal balanced consistent hashing moves only the new owner’s share.
- Distributed placement needs an agreed stable hash and configuration.

## Further reading
- [Consistent hashing original paper](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall09/cos518/papers/chash.pdf)

questions.prompt: A cache cluster places each key on server `hash(key) % N` using a stable hash. It runs at a 95% hit rate on ten servers. Right after an eleventh server is added, the hit rate collapses and the database is flooded. What best explains this?

options.text: Only the new server's share of keys moved, about one key in eleven
options.explanation: That is the ideal for consistent hashing. With remainder placement, changing the divisor changes the remainder for most keys.

options.text: About half the keys moved, as when doubling the server count
options.explanation: Roughly half applies when the divisor doubles. Adding one server to ten moves far more.

options.text: Most keys, about ten in every eleven, now map to a different server whose cache does not hold them
options.explanation: Correct. Under uniform hashes, remainder placement moves all but about one key in every eleven when an eleventh server joins ten: roughly 91% of keys. Those lookups miss until the caches refill.

options.text: The new server corrupted the existing caches
options.explanation: The cached data is untouched. The lookup rule simply points most keys at a server that never stored them.

questions.workedExample:
1. A key's server is its hash's remainder after dividing by the server count. Change the count from 10 to 11 and the remainder changes for most hashes.
2. Under uniform hashes about 10 keys in 11 (roughly 91%) move, so almost every request now goes to a server whose cache is cold.
3. The misses fall through to the database at once, which explains the flood.
4. Consistent hashing would ideally move only the new server's share, about 1 key in 11 (9%), keeping most of the cache warm.

lessons.title: Separate chaining and load
lessons.summary: Chaining keeps a small list per bucket, so it tolerates load factors above one and slows down gradually.
lessons.body:
However good the hash function, two keys will eventually want the same bucket. For independent uniform bucket choices, with 23 keys in 365 buckets the chance of at least one collision is already over 50% (the **birthday paradox**: 23 people in a room probably include two who share a birthday). So the real design question for a hash table is not *whether* collisions happen but *what to do* when they do.

There are two families of answer. **Separate chaining** lets a bucket hold many keys. **Open addressing** keeps one key per slot and, on a collision, looks for another slot in the same array.

## Separate chaining

Each bucket holds a small collection, usually a linked list, of every key that hashed there.

```
idx  bucket
 0   -> [k7]
 1   (empty)
 2   -> [k2] -> [k9] -> [k4]
 3   -> [k5]
```

- **Insert**: hash, then add to that bucket's list (after checking the key is not already there).
- **Look up**: hash, then scan that one list.
- **Delete**: unlink the node. Nothing else in the table is affected.

How long is a chain? Assume **simple uniform hashing** (every key is equally likely to land in any bucket, independently of the others). Then the average chain length is just the load factor: keys divided by buckets. A lookup for an absent key reaches its bucket and scans that whole chain, so its expected cost is about one step plus the load factor. A lookup for a present key stops partway along its chain, so it costs a little less on average. The practical message: chaining's cost grows *linearly* with the load factor, with no cliff as the table fills.

```formula reference
S_miss ≈ 1 + α
S_hit = 2 + (n − 1) / (2m)
where
S_miss: the expected steps for an unsuccessful lookup (key absent): reach the bucket, then scan its whole chain
S_hit: the expected steps for a lookup of a uniformly chosen stored key: reach the bucket, compare the matching key, plus on average half of the other keys sharing its bucket
α: alpha, the load factor n / m, the average number of keys per bucket
n: the number of keys stored
m: the number of buckets
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a miss costs about one step plus the average chain length; a hit costs about two steps plus half the other keys likely to share its bucket. Both grow in a straight line with the load.
```

The "1" is the cost of computing the hash and reaching the bucket. These are averages: an unlucky or attacked table can still put many keys in one chain.

Chaining is simple and degrades gracefully: α can go above 1 (more keys than buckets) and the table still works, just more slowly. Its costs are memory and locality. In a node-based linked-list implementation, each entry has a `next` pointer and may live in a separate allocation. Following those pointers can incur cache misses; their importance depends on representation and workload.

Java's `HashMap`, common C++ `std::unordered_map` implementations and many textbook tables use chaining. The C++ standard specifies bucket and reference-stability requirements, without mandating one physical layout.

## Capacity versus collision strategy

Linear probing, double hashing and Robin Hood hashing are all open-addressing designs: one slot holds at most one key. Rearranging keys or changing the next candidate slot does not create extra storage. Separate chaining can store more keys than buckets because each bucket owns a collection rather than a single-key slot. Later units examine how the open-addressing sequences work, but this capacity distinction already follows from where entries live.

## Key takeaways
- Each bucket holds a collection, so the load factor can exceed one.
- Expected chain costs assume uniform hashing and a randomly selected successful key.
- Per-node pointers and cache misses are important practical costs.

## Further reading
- [Open addressing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_addressing)

questions.prompt: You need to store 12 keys in a table with 8 buckets and you are not allowed to resize. Which scheme can do it?

options.text: Separate chaining
options.explanation: Correct. Each bucket holds a list, so 8 buckets can hold any number of keys. The load factor is 1.5: chains average one and a half keys, so lookups are slower than at a lower load but still work.

options.text: Linear probing
options.explanation: Open addressing stores one key per slot, so 8 slots hold at most 8 keys. The 9th insert has nowhere to go.

options.text: Double hashing
options.explanation: Still open addressing: at most one key per slot, so 8 slots cap the table at 8 keys.

options.text: Robin Hood hashing
options.explanation: Robin Hood rearranges keys within an open-addressed array but cannot exceed one key per slot.

questions.workedExample:
1. Open addressing (linear, quadratic, double hashing, Robin Hood) puts every key in its own array slot, so there can never be more keys than slots, and in practice the table is kept well below full.
2. Chaining lets any number of keys share a bucket. Twelve keys in eight buckets give a load factor of 1.5: under uniform hashing, chains average 1.5 keys.
3. A lookup for an absent key then scans about 1.5 keys after reaching its bucket, instead of about 0.75 at a load of 0.75. Slower, but the table still works.
4. That graceful degradation is one reason chaining is a common default.

lessons.title: Linear probing and clustering
lessons.summary: Linear probing steps to the next slot on a collision; clusters form, and miss cost rises steeply as the table fills.
lessons.body:
Open addressing keeps every entry inside the slot array itself. Linear probing is its simplest form, and it shows the central trade-off of the whole family: excellent locality while the table has room, and a sharp slowdown as it fills.

## Open addressing

All keys live directly in the array, one per slot. To insert, you follow the key's **probe sequence**, a fixed list of slots to try in order (first choice, second choice, …), until you find an empty slot. A lookup follows the same sequence until it finds the key or hits an empty slot, which proves the key is absent: had it been inserted, it would have stopped there.

Because everything is in one contiguous array, open addressing is compact and cache-friendly. The load factor cannot exceed one: there are no more key positions than slots. Lookups for missing keys stop only at an empty slot, so these tables keep spare slots and grow well before they are full.

### Linear probing

Try the key's **home slot** (the slot its hash picks), then the next slot along, then the next, wrapping round from the end of the array to the start.

Example: a 7-slot table where each key's home slot is its remainder after dividing by 7. Insert 10, 17, 24, 3, 5 (home slots 3, 3, 3, 3, 5):

```
slot  0   1   2   3   4   5   6
      5   .   .   10  17  24  3
```

Four keys wanted slot 3 and spilled into 4, 5 and 6. Then 5, whose home was slot 5, found 5 and 6 taken and wrapped round to slot 0. Any key hashing anywhere into slots 3 to 6 now has to walk to the end of this run.

That is **primary clustering**: occupied runs grow, and a longer run is more likely to be hit and so grows faster. Runs that touch merge into even longer runs.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: parking along a single row
> Each driver is assigned a bay in a long row of numbered bays. If it is taken, they drive on to the next free bay. Early in the day everyone parks at or next to their bay. Late in the day, a block of full bays forms and every driver whose bay is in that block must crawl past it to the end.
>
> **How it maps:** bays are slots, the assigned bay is the home slot and driving on is the probe sequence. The full block is a cluster: the bigger it gets, the more drivers arrive inside it and lengthen it. Checking whether a friend has parked means walking from their bay until you find them or an empty bay.
>
> **Where it stops:** a real car park could put up a sign listing who is where. A hash table has only the slots themselves, and when a car leaves, its bay cannot simply be left empty without breaking other people's searches, which is the subject of the deletion lesson.

### How cost rises with load

Donald Knuth worked out how many slots linear probing examines on average. His formulas assume random, uniformly spread home slots, a large table, and keys that are only inserted (no deletions). In this model a hit costs roughly half of one over the fraction of slots still free, while a miss costs roughly half of one over the *square* of that fraction, so misses grow much faster as the table fills. That is why open-addressing tables resize long before they fill:

```formula reference
P_hit ≈ ½ × (1 + 1 / (1 − α))
P_miss ≈ ½ × (1 + 1 / (1 − α)^2)
where
P_hit: the expected number of slots examined by a successful search (key present)
P_miss: the expected number of slots examined by an unsuccessful search (key absent), which must reach an empty slot
α: alpha, the load factor: the fraction of slots occupied, between 0 and 1
½: one half
^: "to the power of"; (1 − α)^2 is (1 − α) multiplied by itself
≈: approximately equal to (the formulas are averages for large tables)
In words: everything depends on the fraction of slots still free. As it shrinks towards zero, a hit costs roughly half of one over that fraction and a miss roughly half of one over its square, so misses blow up first and fastest.
```

| Fullness | Hit | Miss |
|---|---|---|
| 50% | 1.5 | 2.5 |
| 75% | 2.5 | 8.5 |
| 90% | 5.5 | 50.5 |

Going from 75% full to 90% full makes the modelled miss cost about six times larger, while the hit cost only a little more than doubles. These are model averages, not timings: with tombstones from deletions, or patterned keys, real costs can be worse.

Despite clustering, linear probing often performs very well at moderate load, because consecutive slots usually sit in the same cache line and the processor fetches them together. Measure your implementation and workload rather than assuming either way.

## Key takeaways
- Linear probing continues into adjacent slots and wraps at the end.
- Occupied runs cause primary clustering.
- Knuth’s probe estimates concern a particular random insertion model without deletions.

## Further reading
- [Linear probing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_probing)

lessons.title: Quadratic probing and double hashing
lessons.summary: Quadratic probing and double hashing break up clusters, but table size and step choice decide whether every slot can be reached.
lessons.body:
Linear probing's clusters come from every colliding key taking the same one-slot steps. The fixes in this lesson change the step pattern. But a probe sequence must do more than spread collisions: it must be able to reach a free slot, and the table size and step pattern together decide whether it can.

## Quadratic probing

Instead of stepping one slot at a time, jump by growing amounts: successive retries land 1, 4, 9, 16, … slots from home (the squares), wrapping round the array. Runs no longer merge so readily.

```formula reference
h(k, i) = (h(k) + c_1 i + c_2 i^2) mod m
where
h(k, i): the slot tried on attempt i for key k
h(k): the key's home slot
k: the key being placed or looked up
i: the attempt number, counting from 0
c_1: a fixed constant multiplying the attempt number (0 in the plain "i squared" version)
c_2: a fixed non-zero constant multiplying the attempt number squared (1 in the plain version)
m: the number of slots
mod: "modulo", the remainder after division, which wraps round the array
^: "to the power of"; i^2 = i × i
In words: the distance from home grows with the square of the attempt number, so successive retries spread further and further apart.
```

This removes primary clustering but leaves **secondary clustering**: keys with the same home slot still follow the identical sequence.

Quadratic probing also may not visit every slot. In a 7-slot table, a key homed at slot 0 tries 0, 1, 4, 2, 2, 4, 1, 0, … and never reaches slots 3, 5 or 6. There is a useful guarantee, though: when the number of slots is an odd prime, the first half (rounded up) of the squared-offset probes are all different. So if the table is less than half full, one of those probes must be free and the insert succeeds. Arbitrary choices of the constants have no such guarantee.

A popular variant steps by **triangular numbers** (0, 1, 3, 6, 10, …, each one more step than the last), which visits every slot exactly once when the table size is a power of two. In an 8-slot table those offsets land on slots 0, 1, 3, 6, 2, 7, 5, 4: all eight.

### Double hashing

Use a second hash to choose each key's step size. Each retry moves one more step of that size from home, wrapping round:

```formula reference
h(k, i) = (h_1(k) + i h_2(k)) mod m
where
h(k, i): the slot tried on attempt i for key k
h_1(k): the first hash, giving the home slot
h_2(k): the second hash, giving this key's step size
k: the key
i: the attempt number, counting from 0
m: the number of slots
mod: "modulo", the remainder after division
In words: start at the home slot and move by a key-specific step on each failed attempt, wrapping round the array.
```

Keys with the same home slot now usually follow different sequences, reducing clustering when the two hashes distribute keys well; keys sharing both hashes still share a sequence. Two rules: the step must never be 0 (or you probe the same slot forever), and it must be **coprime** with the table size (share no factor with it other than 1) so the sequence can reach every slot. For a prime table size, any step that is not a multiple of it works; for a power-of-two size, any odd step works.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: guests searching a hotel corridor for a free room
> Hotel guests whose assigned room is taken all try the next door along, so they bunch up at the same few doors: that is linear probing. Double hashing gives each guest a personal jump length, say every third door or every fifth, so guests with the same first choice fan out.
>
> **How it maps:** the first-choice room is the home slot and the jump length is the second hash's step. A jump length that shares a factor with the number of doors, like every second door in a corridor of 16, only ever visits half the rooms, which is why the step must be coprime with the table size.
>
> **Where it stops:** a guest could simply read the vacancy board. A hash table has no board: the same jumps have to be retraced on every later lookup, so the step must be a fixed function of the key.

For the same keys as the linear-probing example (10, 17, 24, 3, 5 into 7 slots, home slot `k % 7`), use the step `5 - k % 5`, which is always between 1 and 5:

```
slot  0   1   2   3   4   5   6
      .   5   .   10  24  3   17
```

17 jumps 3 slots to slot 6, and 24 steps 1 slot to slot 4, rather than all queuing behind 10. The price is computing a second hash and losing the cache locality of linear steps.

## Key takeaways
- Quadratic sequences need table-size and coefficient conditions for coverage.
- Double hashing uses a nonzero step coprime to table size.
- Power-of-two tables need odd double-hash steps for complete coverage.

## Further reading
- [Open addressing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_addressing)
- [Double hashing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_hashing)

25   3     1+25%7 = 5  3+5 = 8 (free)

| 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 4 | 4 |

| 4 | 16 | 2 |

lessons.title: Deletion, tombstones and rebuilding
lessons.summary: Deleting from an open-addressed table needs a tombstone (or shifting) so later keys stay reachable, and tombstones eventually force a rebuild.
lessons.body:
An empty slot proves a search can stop only if insertion would also have stopped there. Deleting an intermediate entry must preserve that argument for entries further along the probe path.

## Deletion and tombstones

Deletion is where open addressing gets subtle. In the earlier seven-slot linear-probing example, keys 10, 17 and 24 (all homed at slot 3) occupy slots 3, 4 and 5. Suppose you delete 17 by setting slot 4 back to empty. A lookup for 24 starts at slot 3 (10, not a match), moves to slot 4, finds it empty, and concludes 24 is absent. Wrong: 24 sits in slot 5.

The fix is a **tombstone**: a special marker meaning "deleted, keep probing".

- **Lookups** skip over tombstones.
- **Inserts** may reuse the first tombstone they pass, but must still probe on to an empty slot to be sure the key is not already further along.

The two methods below are fragments of a table class. `EMPTY` and `TOMB` are unique marker objects, not stored keys, and `_probe(key)` yields the key's slot indices in probe order, at most one full cycle of the table:

```python
EMPTY, TOMB = object(), object()

def get(self, key):
    for i in self._probe(key):
        k = self.keys[i]
        # Only a never-used slot ends a
        # search.
        if k is EMPTY:
            raise KeyError(key)
        if k is not TOMB and k == key:
            return self.vals[i]
    raise KeyError(key)

def delete(self, key):
    for i in self._probe(key):
        k = self.keys[i]
        # Only a never-used slot ends a
        # search.
        if k is EMPTY:
            raise KeyError(key)
        if k is not TOMB and k == key:
            # Preserve later keys' probe
            # paths.
            self.keys[i] = TOMB
            return
    raise KeyError(key)
```

> [!warning] Tombstones pile up
> Tombstones count against the load for lookups, since searches must walk past them, but they hold no data. A table with heavy insert and delete churn can fill with tombstones, making misses slow even though it holds few live keys. Implementations track them and rebuild the table (rehash live keys into a fresh array) when they pass a threshold. In CPython 3.14 ordinary combined dicts, GIL-enabled builds can reuse dummy index slots; dense entry holes are generally compacted on rebuild. Free-threaded builds do not reuse dummy index slots, and popitem can trim the dense entry tail.

With linear probing there is an alternative: **backward-shift deletion**. After emptying a slot, scan forward and move back any key that could legally sit in the gap, until you reach an empty slot. No tombstones, at the cost of more work per delete.

## Follow the stopping proof

After deleting a key, ask what a future lookup will conclude at that slot. An empty marker says "no search ever needed to continue past here". A tombstone says "a search may once have continued past here, so keep going". Neither slot holds a live entry, but they make different promises.

The fragments also handle two edge cases. If the probe generator runs through a full cycle without meeting an empty slot, the key is absent, so both methods raise `KeyError` after the loop. A complete insert method, not shown, must update an existing key rather than blindly reuse the first tombstone it passes, and must cope with a table that has no truly empty slot left.

## Key takeaways
- An empty marker stops lookup; a tombstone does not.
- Insertion must keep searching for duplicates before reusing a tombstone.
- Deletion churn can require rebuilding even with few live keys.

## Further reading
- [Open addressing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_addressing)

lessons.title: Robin Hood probe distances
lessons.summary: Robin Hood insertion gives a contested slot to the key that has travelled further, shrinking the worst probe distances and letting misses stop early.
lessons.body:
Robin Hood hashing keeps linear probing's layout but changes who gets a contested slot. Its aim is not fewer collisions but a fairer spread of search lengths.

## Robin Hood hashing

Linear probing's average is fine, but its *variance* is the problem: some unlucky keys end up dozens of slots from home. Robin Hood hashing (Celis, Larson and Munro, 1985) evens this out by "taking from the rich and giving to the poor".

Each key's **probe distance** is how far it sits from its home slot, counting forward and wrapping round the end of the array. A key homed at slot 6 that ended up in slot 1 of an 8-slot table travelled 6 → 7 → 0 → 1: distance 3. A key in its home slot has distance 0, so it is "rich"; a key far from home is "poor".

While inserting, if the incoming key has travelled further than the resident of the current slot, they swap: the incoming key takes the slot and the displaced, "richer" key carries on probing.

The fragment below assumes the table has a free slot and the key is not already stored; a complete map must also handle updates to existing keys and grow before it fills.

```python
def rh_insert(slots, key, home):
    # slots hold (key, dist) or None
    m = len(slots)
    i, d = home % m, 0
    while True:
        cur = slots[i]
        if cur is None:
            slots[i] = (key, d)
            return
        # The more displaced key keeps the
        # slot.
        if cur[1] < d:  # resident richer
            slots[i] = (key, d)
            key, d = cur  # carry it on
        i = (i + 1) % m
        d += 1
```

Insert D (home 2), then A, B and C (all home 0):

```
plain linear    A0  B1  D0  C3
robin hood      A0  B1  C2  D1
               (key + probe distance)
```

C reaches slot 2 having travelled 2; D there has travelled 0, so C takes the slot and D moves on to slot 3. The total distance is the same (4), but the worst case drops from 3 to 2. Robin Hood hashing can reduce probe-distance variance; worst-case lookup remains O(n) under adversarial collisions.

It also speeds up misses. Probing for an absent key, you can stop as soon as you meet a resident whose distance is smaller than your current distance: had your key been present, it would have displaced that resident. Deletion usually uses backward shifting.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: giving the seat to whoever has walked furthest
> Passengers board a long train and walk forward looking for a seat. The rule: if you reach a seat whose occupant has walked a shorter distance from their boarding door than you, you take it, and they get up and continue forward. The rule creates no extra seats, so the total walking stays the same, but the longest walks get shorter.
>
> **How it maps:** a passenger's boarding door is the home slot, distance walked is probe distance, and the swap is the Robin Hood rule. The total probe distance is shared out differently rather than reduced (with linear probing the set of occupied slots, and so the total, does not depend on who wins each swap): the longest distances shrink.
>
> **Where it stops:** passengers can see down the carriage; the table compares only with the one resident in the current slot. And if every key shares one home slot, the run is still long: the worst case remains linear.

Rust's standard `HashMap` used Robin Hood hashing until 2019 (Rust 1.36), when it switched to a Swiss-table design from the `hashbrown` crate.

## Key takeaways
- A more displaced incoming key takes a slot from a less displaced resident.
- The swap can reduce probe-distance variance while keeping linear adversarial worst cases.
- An absent-key search can stop at a resident with smaller distance.

## Further reading
- [Hash table: Robin Hood hashing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_table#Robin_Hood_hashing)

options.explanation: Correct. Q displaces X at slot 1, and R displaces X again at slot 2, leaving X two slots from home. Maximum distance is 2 instead of 3.

questions.workedExample:
Rule: at each slot, if the resident's distance is less than the incoming key's, swap and carry the resident onwards.

```
X: slot 1 empty        -> X@1 d0
P: slot 0 empty        -> P@0 d0
Q: s0 P d0 vs Q d0: no
   s1 X d0 < Q d1: swap
   Q@1 d1, carry X
   s2 empty -> X@2 d1
R: s0 P d0 vs R d0: no
   s1 Q d1 vs R d1: no
   s2 X d1 < R d2: swap
   R@2 d2, carry X
   s3 empty -> X@3 d2
```

Final: `P0 Q1 R2 X2`. Total distance is 5, the same as plain linear probing (0 + 0 + 2 + 3), but the maximum falls from 3 to 2: Robin Hood redistributes distance rather than reducing it.

questions.prompt: In a Robin Hood table, you look up an absent key Z whose home is slot 0. The table holds `P0 Q1 R2 X2` in slots 0 to 3, and slot 4 is empty. At which slot can the search stop, and why?

options.text: Slot 3, because X's distance (2) is less than the distance Z would have there (3)
options.explanation: Correct. If Z were present, it would have displaced X when it reached slot 3, so Z cannot be anywhere further along. The search stops after 4 probes without needing to reach the empty slot.

options.text: Slot 4, the first empty slot, as in ordinary linear probing
options.explanation: That is correct for plain linear probing, but Robin Hood's invariant allows stopping one slot earlier here, and often much earlier in longer runs.

options.text: Slot 0, because P is not Z
options.explanation: A mismatch at the home slot proves nothing: Z could have been pushed further along by earlier keys.

options.text: Slot 2, because R also has home slot 0
options.explanation: Matching home slots are expected in a run. The test is whether the resident's distance is *smaller* than the searcher's; at slot 2 both are 2.

questions.workedExample:
1. Track Z's would-be distance d as you probe, and compare with each resident's distance.

```
slot 0: P d0, Z d0 -> keep going
slot 1: Q d1, Z d1 -> keep going
slot 2: R d2, Z d2 -> keep going
slot 3: X d2, Z d3 -> 2 < 3, stop
```

2. Why it is safe: insertion swaps whenever the resident is richer (smaller distance). Had Z been inserted, at slot 3 it would have had distance 3 against X's 2 and taken the slot.
3. So Z is absent. In long, dense runs this early exit saves many probes on misses, which is where linear probing is weakest.

lessons.title: Swiss tables and collision trade-offs
lessons.summary: Swiss tables compare one-byte hash fingerprints for a whole group at once, touching full keys only for likely matches.
lessons.body:
Metadata can make a table search cheap before it touches a key or value. Swiss tables use short hash fingerprints to reject most slots in a group; a fingerprint match still requires checking the real key.

## Modern designs: Swiss tables

Google's **Swiss tables** (Abseil `flat_hash_map`, presented at CppCon in 2017 and open-sourced in Abseil in 2018) are open addressing with a twist. Alongside the slots is an array of one-byte **control bytes**, each holding "empty", "deleted" or 7 bits of the key's hash. On Abseil's x86 SSE2 path, a lookup loads 16 control bytes and uses SIMD instructions to compare all 16 against the key's 7 bits in a single step, only touching the slots that match. Tables run at up to 7/8 full while lookups stay fast.

Rust (via the `hashbrown` crate) and, since Go 1.24, Go's built-in map use Swiss-table designs; Go uses eight-slot groups, so Swiss-table designs do not all probe 16 slots.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: scanning name-badge initials
> Looking for "Priya Shah" among a row of sixteen people wearing badges, you first glance along the row for the initials P.S. and only read the full badge of the one or two people who match.
>
> **How it maps:** the initials are the 7-bit fingerprint in each control byte, the glance along the row is the single SIMD comparison over a group, and reading the full badge is the equality check on the real key.
>
> **Where it stops:** a person glances along the row one badge at a time, very quickly; the processor genuinely compares all sixteen control bytes in one instruction. And a matching pair of initials proves nothing, which is why the full key is always checked.

Another option is **cuckoo hashing**, where each key has two possible slots and an insert pushes a resident out to that resident's alternative slot. The classic two-hash, single-slot, no-stash version checks at most two candidate slots; insertion can trigger rehashing. Bucketed or stashed variants have different lookup bounds.

## Choosing between them

| | Chaining | Open addressing |
|---|---|---|
| Load factor | can exceed 1 | at most 1; normally kept below it |
| Memory | node + pointer each | one flat array |
| Cache behaviour | pointer chasing | contiguous |
| Delete | trivial | tombstones or shifting |
| Near full | slows gently | slows sharply |

Chaining is the safer general-purpose choice when keys are large or the load is unpredictable, and it lets you swap the chain for a tree (Java HashMap: splitting and tree bins). Open addressing can offer good locality and low overhead at controlled load; actual speed depends on key size, hash cost and workload.

## Fingerprints are candidates, not equality

A seven-bit fingerprint has only 128 possible values. Several distinct keys can therefore match the same control byte. The vector comparison creates a shortlist; the table still checks the actual key for every surviving candidate. The control-byte shortcut reduces unnecessary memory accesses without changing the equality contract.

Deletion markers and empty markers also remain distinct metadata states. A lookup can use an empty marker to establish a stopping condition according to the table’s probing rules; a deleted slot may require continuing to another group. Group width is a property of the implementation and hardware path, so copying a statement about Abseil’s sixteen-byte comparison to every Swiss-table implementation would be wrong.

When comparing designs, measure the workload you actually have. Small inline keys and values benefit from a flat layout differently from large objects reached through pointers. The hash computation itself can dominate when keys are long, and references into a flat container may have different stability guarantees from references into a node-based container. Choose the API contract as well as a favourable average probe count.

## Key takeaways
- Swiss-table metadata rejects most candidate slots before touching full keys.
- Fingerprint matches still need equality checks.
- Group widths and reference stability depend on the implementation.

## Further reading
- [Swiss tables design notes — Abseil](https://abseil.io/about/design/swisstables)
- [Cuckoo hashing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuckoo_hashing)
- [Go Swiss-table implementation](https://go.dev/blog/swisstable)

questions.prompt: A Swiss-table control-byte fingerprint matches the query. What should lookup do next?

options.text: Return the value without checking the key
options.explanation: Different keys can share a short fingerprint, so returning without equality can return the wrong entry.

options.text: Check the real key for equality
options.explanation: Correct: a fingerprint match only identifies a candidate for equality checking.

options.text: Reject the key because the fingerprint is short
options.explanation: A short matching fingerprint is a useful candidate, not a reason to reject it.

options.text: Always rebuild the table
options.explanation: Fingerprint matches are normal; they do not require rebuilding.

questions.workedExample: A short fingerprint only identifies candidates. Distinct full keys can share the same seven-bit fingerprint, so the table must still check equality. SIMD helps shortlist candidates rather than replacing that check.

questions.prompt: Which statements about chaining and open addressing are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Linear probing can benefit from locality because it examines consecutive array slots
options.explanation: Correct. Linear probing in particular often finds the key within the same cache line, whereas chaining follows pointers to scattered heap nodes.

options.text: Deleting from a chained table requires tombstones
options.explanation: No: in chaining you simply unlink the node from its list. Tombstones are an open-addressing technique.

options.text: Linear probing suffers primary clustering; quadratic probing still has secondary clustering
options.explanation: Correct. Quadratic probing breaks up runs, but keys with the same home slot follow the same jump sequence.

options.text: Double hashing makes two keys with the same home slot follow the same probe sequence
options.explanation: The opposite: the second hash gives them (usually) different step sizes, which is its whole purpose.

options.text: A chained table keeps working with more stored keys than buckets
options.explanation: Chaining permits more entries than buckets, subject to memory limits; expected scan cost grows with load.

questions.workedExample:
Go through each statement:

1. **Cache-friendliness**: linear probing touches nearby array slots; other probing sequences need not. True.
2. **Chaining deletions**: removing a list node does not affect any other key's lookup path. False.
3. **Clustering**: linear probing builds runs that merge (primary); quadratic probing jumps, but identical home slots share a sequence (secondary). True.
4. **Double hashing**: a second hash can give different steps, though some pairs still share a sequence. False.
5. **Chaining with more keys than buckets** (load factor above 1): valid, just slower. True.

lessons.title: Load-factor limits and space trade-offs
lessons.summary: The maximum load factor trades empty slots against collision work, and the right limit depends on how the table resolves collisions.
lessons.body:
A hash table's speed depends on one ratio: its **load factor**, the number of stored keys divided by the number of buckets. Keep it low and buckets are mostly empty or hold a single key, so operations are fast. Let it creep up and chains lengthen or probe runs grow.

Many dynamically growing tables therefore watch the load factor and, when it passes a **maximum load factor**, allocate a bigger array and move everything across. This lesson is about choosing that limit; the following lessons cover the move itself. The key point: a useful limit depends on how the table resolves collisions, so a chaining table and a probing table need not share the same threshold.

## Choosing the maximum load factor

The threshold is a space–time trade-off. A low maximum wastes memory on empty slots; a high one makes operations slower.

| Table | Typical/default growth policy | Scheme |
|---|---|---|
| Java `HashMap` | 0.75 | chaining |
| CPython `dict` | about 2/3 | open addressing |
| Abseil Swiss table | 7/8 | open addressing + SIMD |
| Redis dict | normally grows near 1; policy can defer growth | chaining |

Chaining tolerates a higher load factor because a slightly longer chain is a mild slowdown: cost grows in a straight line with load. Open addressing is far more sensitive. In Knuth's model for linear probing (Linear probing and clustering), the expected cost of a miss depends on one over the *square* of the free fraction of slots. Going from 3/4 full to 7/8 full halves the free fraction, so it roughly quadruples the expected miss cost: from about 8.5 probes to about 32.5.

That model assumes random hashing, plain linear probing and no deletions; it is not the formula for every probing design. Swiss tables can run at 7/8 full because they probe whole groups of slots at once, comparing one-byte metadata entries first, so few probes ever touch the slots themselves.

In Java, the default maximum load factor of 0.75 with 16 buckets gives a threshold of 12 entries. Ordinary `put` grows the table only once the size goes *above* that threshold, so the 13th new key triggers the first doubling.

## Key takeaways
- Growth limits trade empty capacity against collision work.
- Chaining, linear probing and group probing need different cost models.
- Java’s ordinary size-triggered growth occurs after exceeding its threshold.

## Further reading
- [Hash table: dynamic resizing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_table#Dynamic_resizing)
- [Amortized analysis — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amortized_analysis)

questions.prompt: A Java `HashMap` has 16 buckets and the default load factor of 0.75. Which `put` of a new key triggers the first resize? Assume well-distributed hashes, so collisions do not trigger an earlier resize.

options.text: The 12th
options.explanation: 12 is the threshold (16 × 0.75), but Java resizes when the size goes *above* the threshold, so the 12th entry still fits.

options.text: The 13th
options.explanation: Correct. Sixteen buckets at the default maximum load factor give a threshold of twelve entries. The thirteenth new entry exceeds it, doubling the table to thirty-two buckets.

options.text: The 16th
options.explanation: This assumes the table fills completely. A chaining table could, but Java resizes at 75% load to keep chains short.

options.text: The 17th
options.explanation: This assumes resizing only when there are more entries than buckets (a load factor above 1), which is not Java's rule.

questions.workedExample:
1. The threshold is capacity × maximum load factor: 16 buckets × 0.75 = 12 entries.
2. Java's `putVal` ends with `if (++size > threshold) resize();`, a strict "greater than".
3. Inserts 1 to 12: the size never exceeds 12, so no resize.
4. Insert 13: the size becomes 13, which is greater than 12, so the table doubles to 32 buckets (new threshold 24).
5. The off-by-one matters when pre-sizing: a threshold equal to your expected count is just enough.

lessons.title: Rehashing and geometric growth
lessons.summary: Growing a table re-places every entry because bucket choice depends on size, yet geometric growth keeps the copying to a constant per insert on average.
lessons.body:
When a table passes its maximum load factor it allocates a bigger array. This lesson covers what moving into that array costs, and why the cost still averages out to a constant per insert.

## Rehashing: why every key moves

You cannot copy the old array across as it is, because a key's bucket depends on the table size: the bucket is the full hash's remainder after dividing by the number of buckets. The full hash never changes, but the divisor does. A key with hash 14 lives in bucket 2 of a 4-bucket table but bucket 6 of an 8-bucket table.

```
old m = 4         new m = 8
hash  idx         hash  idx
  5    1            5    5
  9    1            9    1
 14    2           14    6
```

Doubling the table moves about half the keys under uniform hashing, but the table cannot know which half without looking. Growing therefore means **rehashing**: walking every entry and inserting it into the new array.

Visiting and copying the entries costs O(n) for n entries; placing them by ordinary probing is expected O(n) with well-distributed hashes, and collision-heavy reinsertion can cost more. An implementation can store each entry's full hash so it does not recompute it (which matters for long strings), but every entry must still be visited and placed.

## Amortised analysis: why inserts are still O(1)

One O(n) insert sounds bad. The trick is that, if the table grows by a constant **factor**, expensive inserts become rarer as the table grows.

Picture a table that starts with one slot and doubles when full. The resizes copy 1 key, then 2, then 4, 8, and so on. Each resize copies more than all the earlier ones put together, so the last resize does about half of all the copying ever done. Inserting 1,024 keys this way causes only 1,023 copies in total: about one per insert.

```formula reference
C < 2n
T = C + n < 3n
where
C: the total number of key copies made by all the resizes together
T: the combined copying and placement work, in unit operations
n: the positive number of keys inserted; each initial placement costs one unit in this model
<: is strictly less than
In words: geometric growth copies fewer than two keys per insert overall, so copying plus placing costs fewer than three units per insert on average, for any number of inserts.
```

Thus **resizing overhead** is amortised O(1) per insert, for every sequence of inserts, not just on average over random inputs. The overall cost of a hash-table insert also includes collision work, so the usual statement is *expected* amortised O(1), assuming well-distributed hashes and constant-time key operations. The same doubling argument applies to dynamic arrays (Arrays, Lists, Stacks & Queues).

## Key takeaways
- Changing capacity changes bucket reduction and requires visiting all entries.
- Geometric growth keeps total copying proportional to the insertion count.
- Amortised copying bounds do not prove bounded individual latency or collision cost.

## Further reading
- [Hash table: dynamic resizing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_table#Dynamic_resizing)
- [Amortized analysis — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amortized_analysis)

questions.prompt: When a hash table grows from 8 to 16 buckets, why can't it just copy the old array into the first half of the new one?

options.text: A key's bucket depends on table size, so some keys may need a different bucket
options.explanation: Correct. A key with hash 13 sits in bucket 5 of an 8-bucket table (13 leaves remainder 5 when divided by 8), but lookups in the 16-bucket table will look in bucket 13. Each key must be re-placed according to the new size.

options.text: Copying arrays is slower than re-inserting
options.explanation: A block copy does not put moved entries in the buckets the new lookup rule expects; speed depends on implementation.

options.text: Keys must be sorted during the resize
options.explanation: Sorting is not required to redistribute entries. Some bucket implementations can have an internal ordering.

options.text: The hash function changes when the table grows
options.explanation: The hash value is the same; it is the reduction to an index (`mod m` or `& (m − 1)`) that changes with m.

questions.workedExample:
1. The bucket is the key's hash reduced by the table size: the remainder after dividing by the number of buckets (or, for a power-of-two size, the hash's low bits).
2. Hash 13 gives bucket 5 in an 8-bucket table but bucket 13 in a 16-bucket table. The hash itself did not change; the divisor did.
3. If you simply copied the old array into the first half of the new one, the key would stay at index 5, but `get` would compute 13 and miss it.
4. So every key is rehashed (re-placed) into the new array: O(n) visiting and copying work for n keys, with expected linear placement under suitable collision assumptions. Storing each entry's full hash avoids recomputing it, but not the re-placement.

questions.prompt: For a doubling hash table, what does amortised O(1) resizing overhead guarantee, considering only entry-copying work?

options.text: Every insert takes constant time
options.explanation: That is a worst-case O(1) guarantee. An insert that triggers a resize takes O(n).

options.text: Inserts take O(1) on average over random inputs
options.explanation: That describes average-case analysis over inputs. Amortised analysis is about the total cost of any *sequence* of operations, not a probability over inputs.

options.text: Any sequence of n inserts from an empty table incurs O(n) total copying, although individual resizes can be expensive
options.explanation: Correct. The rare O(n) resizes are paid for by the many cheap inserts around them, so the average per operation over the sequence is constant.

options.text: Inserts are O(1) once the table has stopped growing
options.explanation: Amortised O(1) covers the growing phase too; that is its whole point.

questions.workedExample:
1. Amortised analysis looks at the total cost of a whole *sequence* of operations, then divides by the number of operations. No probability is involved.
2. Start from one slot and double when full. The resizes copy 1, 2, 4, 8, … keys. Each copy is bigger than all earlier ones combined, so the total stays below twice the number of inserts.
3. Add one unit per insert for placing the new key and the whole sequence costs fewer than three units per insert, even though one particular insert (the one that triggers the last resize) visits every live key.
4. For example, 1,000 inserts trigger copies of 1, 2, 4, …, 512 keys: 1,023 copies in all.
5. Collision work and key operations remain separate costs, and a single resize can still cause a noticeable pause; amortised O(1) is not a real-time guarantee.

questions.prompt: A table starts with capacity 1 and doubles whenever it is full. You instrument it while inserting 1,000,000 keys and log every key moved during a resize. What will the log show?

options.text: About as many moves as inserts in total, with the last few resizes accounting for most of them
options.explanation: Correct. Resizes copy 1, 2, 4, …, 524,288 keys: 1,048,575 moves in all, about one per insert. The final resize alone moves about half of them.

options.text: About 20 moves, one per resize
options.explanation: About 20 is the number of resizes (the number of doublings from 1 to a million). Each resize moves every key present, not just one.

options.text: About 20 million moves, because every resize moves all million keys
options.explanation: Early resizes happen when the table is tiny and move very few keys. The sizes form a doubling series, so the total stays close to the final size.

options.text: About 500 billion moves, because each insert eventually moves every earlier key
options.explanation: That quadratic total is what happens if the table grows by one slot at a time. Doubling avoids it.

questions.workedExample:
1. A resize happens when the table is full, and it moves every key present.
2. The capacities at which resizes happen are 1, 2, 4, …, 524,288; after that the capacity of 1,048,576 is enough for a million keys.
3. A doubling series adds up to just under twice its last term: 524,288 × 2 − 1 = 1,048,575 moves. That is about one move per insert, and the last resize alone is half the total.
4. Adding the million initial placements gives about 2 units of work per insert: amortised O(1). The cost is concentrated in a few big pauses, which is the subject of the incremental-rehashing lesson.

lessons.title: Growth increments, shrinking and pause limits
lessons.summary: Grow by a factor, shrink with a hysteresis gap, and use incremental rehashing when one long resize pause is unacceptable.
lessons.body:
Geometric growth makes resizing cheap *on average*. This lesson covers three practical refinements: why the growth must be by a factor rather than a fixed amount, how to shrink without thrashing, and what to do when even one long pause is unacceptable.

## Fixed increments versus geometric growth

Growing by a constant **amount** does not work. Add 10 slots each time and every resize copies 10 more keys than the last. For n keys there is a resize every 10 inserts, and the later ones each copy most of the table, so the total copying grows with the square of n and the cost per insert keeps rising as the table grows: O(n) amortised rather than O(1). The program below counts the copies exactly for both policies:

```python
def total_copies(n, grow):
    cap, size, copies = 1, 0, 0
    for _ in range(n):
        if size == cap:
            # Count only moves, not hash
            # work.
            copies += size
            cap = grow(cap)
        size += 1
    return copies

total_copies(1000, lambda c: 2 * c)
# 1023
total_copies(1000, lambda c: c + 10)
# 49600
```

Doubling copies 1,023 keys for 1,000 inserts, about one each; adding 10 slots at a time copies 49,600, about 50 each, and that per-insert figure keeps climbing as n grows.

> [!note] The banker's view
> Charge each insert 3 units instead of 1. One pays for the insert itself; two are saved. Between doublings, half the old capacity in new inserts earns two saved units per insert: enough to pay for moving every key in the full old table. No operation ever runs up a debt, so the average stays at 3.

### Shrinking without thrashing

If a table also shrinks when it empties, do not use the same threshold in both directions. Grow when the table is completely full and shrink when it drops below half full, and a workload hovering at the boundary (insert, delete, insert, …) would resize on every operation: a doubled table is exactly half full, so one delete shrinks it, and the shrunken table is full, so one insert doubles it again.

The textbook fix is a **hysteresis gap** (a deliberate difference between the grow and shrink points): double when full, halve only when the table falls to a quarter full. After either resize the table is half full, so at least a quarter of its size in operations must happen before the next one, and those cheap operations pay for it. Many real tables simply never shrink automatically; CPython's dict does not shrink when you delete keys.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a thermostat
> A heating thermostat set to switch on below 19 °C and off above 21 °C does not flick on and off every few seconds when the room sits at 20 °C. If on and off shared a single setting, it would chatter constantly.
>
> **How it maps:** the room temperature is the load factor, switching the heating on or off is growing or shrinking the table, and the gap between 19 °C and 21 °C is the gap between the "full" and "quarter full" thresholds.
>
> **Where it stops:** a thermostat's switching is cheap and the room changes slowly. A resize costs work proportional to the whole table, so the gap must be wide enough that the operations between resizes can pay for that work, which is why the shrink point is a quarter, not just below a half.

### When amortised is not good enough

Amortised O(1) still means an occasional O(n) pause. The pause depends on the implementation, key count, allocator and hardware; measure it against the server's latency budget.

**Incremental rehashing** spreads the work out. Redis keeps two tables during a resize and moves a few buckets on each operation (plus, by default, a little extra work from its periodic housekeeping timer). Lookups check both tables until the move completes. Go's built-in map used a similar gradual "evacuation" before its Go 1.24 redesign. The cost is complexity and, temporarily, retaining both bucket arrays: when doubling, the old array plus one twice its size, so three times the old bucket count (excluding entries and other overhead).

If you know the final size, the simplest fix is to **pre-size** the table to avoid growth for the planned live-key count. Deletion churn can still require compaction/rebuilds.

## Key takeaways
- Fixed capacity increments cause growing amortised copying costs.
- Different grow and shrink thresholds prevent boundary thrashing.
- Incremental migration spreads pauses while temporarily retaining two tables.

## Further reading
- [Hash table: dynamic resizing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_table#Dynamic_resizing)
- [Amortized analysis — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amortized_analysis)

questions.prompt: A hand-written table starts at 1,000 slots and grows by adding 1,000 slots whenever it is full. Loading 1,000,000 keys spends most of its time copying keys during resizes. You now need to load 2,000,000 keys. What happens to the copying cost *per insert*, and what is the fix?

options.text: It stays about the same, because resizing is amortised O(1)
options.explanation: Amortised O(1) needs growth by a constant *factor*. Growing by a fixed amount gives an arithmetic series of copies, whose total grows with the square of the key count.

options.text: It roughly doubles, because each insert pays O(n) amortised; grow by a factor such as 2 instead
options.explanation: Correct. With fixed +1,000 growth, a million keys cost about 500 copies per insert (499.5 million in total) and two million cost about 1,000 per insert. Doubling the capacity instead keeps it near one copy per insert.

options.text: It halves, because larger tables resize less often
options.explanation: The resizes still come every 1,000 inserts, and each one copies more keys than the last, so per-insert cost rises.

options.text: It quadruples, and nothing can be done short of pre-sizing
options.explanation: The *total* roughly quadruples, but that is spread over twice as many inserts, so per-insert cost doubles. Growing by a factor fixes it without knowing the final size in advance.

questions.workedExample:
1. With fixed growth, a resize happens every 1,000 inserts and copies every key present: 1,000, then 2,000, then 3,000, and so on.
2. That is an arithmetic series. Its total grows with the square of the number of keys: about 499.5 million copies for a million keys, about 2 billion for two million.
3. Per insert, that is about 500 copies at a million keys and about 1,000 at two million: double the keys, double the per-insert cost. That is O(n) amortised.
4. Growing by a constant factor (doubling) makes the copies a geometric series whose total is less than twice the number of inserts, so per-insert copying stays constant however large the table grows.

questions.prompt: A table doubles when its load factor (keys ÷ slots) reaches 1 and halves when it drops below ½. A workload sits at exactly the boundary, alternating insert and delete. What goes wrong, and what is the standard fix?

options.text: Nothing: amortised analysis guarantees O(1) per operation
options.explanation: The amortised argument needs many cheap operations between resizes. Here a resize can follow every operation, so there is nothing to amortise against.

options.text: The table runs out of memory
options.explanation: Memory use oscillates between two sizes; it does not grow without bound.

options.text: Lookups return wrong results during the resize
options.explanation: A correct resize rehashes everything; results stay correct. The problem is purely cost.

options.text: Each insert doubles and each delete halves, so every operation costs O(n); shrink only when the load factor falls to ¼
options.explanation: Correct. After growth the table is half full; one delete triggers a shrink, leaving the smaller table full, and reinsertion grows it again. Shrinking only at a quarter full creates a useful gap.

questions.workedExample:
1. Track the load factor (keys ÷ slots) through one cycle, starting with 8 keys just after doubling into 16 slots: 8 ÷ 16 is exactly one half.
2. One delete leaves 7 ÷ 16, below one half, so the table halves to 8 slots. Now 7 keys sit in 8 slots.
3. One insert makes 8 ÷ 8, completely full, so the table doubles again to 16 slots. Each of these resizes rehashes every key.
4. Alternate insert and delete around the boundary and you pay O(n) for n keys on almost every operation: thrashing.
5. Fix: a **hysteresis gap** between the grow and shrink points. Double when full, halve at a quarter full. After either resize the table is half full, so at least a quarter of its size in operations must happen before the next resize, which pays for it.
6. Many production tables (including CPython's dict) never shrink on delete at all.

lessons.title: CPython dictionaries: layout and probing
lessons.summary: CPython's dict pairs a sparse index array with dense insertion-ordered entries, grows at two-thirds full and mixes high hash bits into its probes.
lessons.body:
Python the language promises how a dict behaves, including insertion order. How CPython achieves that is an implementation detail, and it shows how the ideas in this module fit together in a real table. Everything below describes CPython 3.14's ordinary dict with general keys; other Python implementations, and other CPython layouts, can differ.

## How CPython's dict works

CPython's dict is open addressing with a **compact layout**, introduced in Python 3.6 and based on a 2012 proposal by Raymond Hettinger. The simplified description below covers an ordinary combined table with general keys. Split/key-sharing tables and Unicode-only entries have different layouts. There are two arrays:

```
indices (small ints, 1 per slot)
[ -,  1,  -,  0,  -,  -,  2,  - ]

entries (dense, insertion order)
0: hash, 'cat', 1
1: hash, 'dog', 2
2: hash, 'eel', 3
```

- The **indices array** is the hash table proper. Each slot holds an index into `entries`, and uses 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes depending on the table size, so a small dict's index is tiny.
- The **entries array** stores (hash, key, value) in insertion order. That is why dicts preserve insertion order: iteration just walks `entries`.

Compared with the old design, which stored full entries in a sparse array (24 bytes per general entry on the illustrated 64-bit build), this saves a lot of memory, because only the cheap index array is sparse.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a visitors' book with a lookup card
> A reception desk writes each visitor on the next free line of a visitors' book, in arrival order. To find someone quickly, it also keeps a small card of numbered boxes; each box holds just a line number in the book.
>
> **How it maps:** the book is the dense entries array, which is why iteration follows insertion order. The card is the sparse indices array: it can have many empty boxes cheaply, because each box holds only a small line number rather than a whole entry.
>
> **Where it stops:** a receptionist would cross out a departed visitor and never reuse the line. CPython also leaves a hole in the entries when you delete, but marks the box on the card as "dummy" so searches keep probing, and compacts the book only when the dict is rebuilt.

Further details:

- **Sizes** are powers of two, minimum 8. A table holds at most two-thirds of its size in entries (CPython's `USABLE_FRACTION`), so an 8-slot dict holds 5 keys.
- **Growth**: when full, the new size is the smallest power of two that is at least three times the number of live keys. Without deletions this doubles the table: in CPython 3.14, a dict built key by key resizes on the 6th, 11th, 22nd and 43rd inserts. Deleting keys never shrinks it.
- **Probing** uses a perturbed sequence, not linear steps, described below.
- **Deletion** marks the index slot as a dummy (a tombstone) and the entry as empty. A rebuild compacts empty entries. In GIL-enabled builds a later insertion can reuse a dummy index slot; free-threaded builds avoid that reuse for lookup safety.

```formula reference
U = floor(2m / 3)
m_new = 2^⌈log_2(3u)⌉
where
U: the usable capacity: the most entries a table of m slots can hold before it must grow
m: the table size (number of index slots), a power of two
m_new: the size of the new table after growing
u: the number of live keys when the table grows
floor: round down to a whole number
log_2: logarithm to base 2, the power 2 must be raised to
⌈ ⌉: ceiling, round up to a whole number
^: "to the power of"
In words: a dict can fill two-thirds of its slots; when it is full it grows to the next power of two that is at least three times its live keys. An 8-slot dict holds 5 keys and grows to 16 slots on the 6th insert.
```

## The perturbed probe sequence

Linear probing in a power-of-two table would look only at the hash's low bits, and keys sharing those bits would form runs. CPython instead mixes the rest of the hash into the first few probes. It keeps a value called `perturb`, starting as the full hash (read as an unsigned 64-bit number), and shifts it right by 5 bits before each step:

```python
def probe_order(h, size, n):
    # size is a power of two
    mask = size - 1
    perturb = h & (2**64 - 1)
    i = h & mask
    out = [i]
    while len(out) < n:
        perturb >>= 5
        i = (5 * i + perturb + 1) & mask
        out.append(i)
    return out

probe_order(1234, 8, 4)  # [2, 1, 7, 4]
```

Here `& mask` keeps the low bits, which for a power-of-two size is the same as the remainder after dividing by the size. For a hash of 1,234 in an 8-slot table, the first slot is 2; `perturb` then shrinks to 38, 1 and 0, steering the next probes to 1, 7 and 4. Keys that share low bits but differ higher up therefore part company after a probe or two.

Once `perturb` reaches 0, the step is just `5*i + 1`, and in a power-of-two table that recurrence visits every slot before repeating, so a search always finds an empty slot eventually.

## Key takeaways
- Ordinary combined dictionaries use sparse indices over insertion-ordered entries.
- Perturbed probing feeds higher hash bits into early probes.
- Capacity, tombstone reuse and layouts are implementation and build details.

## Further reading
- [More compact dictionaries with faster iteration — Raymond Hettinger, python-dev](https://mail.python.org/pipermail/python-dev/2012-December/123028.html)
- [CPython 3.14 dictionary implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/3.14/Objects/dictobject.c)

lessons.title: Java HashMap: splitting and tree bins
lessons.summary: Java's HashMap folds high hash bits into the index, splits each chain in one pass when doubling, and turns very long chains into trees.
lessons.body:
Java's `HashMap` is a chaining table with three refinements worth knowing: it mixes high hash bits into the bucket index, it splits chains cheaply when it doubles, and it turns very long chains into balanced trees. This lesson follows OpenJDK 21's ordinary `put` and resize paths.

## How Java's HashMap works

Java's `HashMap` uses separate chaining over an array whose length is always a power of two (default 16).

**Spreading the hash.** In Java's source the bucket index is `(n - 1) & hash`, where `n` is the table length (not the number of keys) and `&` is bitwise AND. Because the length is a power of two, this keeps the hash's low bits, the same as taking its remainder after dividing by the length: a hash of 53 (binary 110101) in a 16-bucket table goes to bucket 5 (binary 0101).

Using only the low bits is fast, but it ignores the high bits. To stop poor `hashCode()` implementations that differ only in their high bits from colliding, Java first mixes the high half into the low half:

```java
static int hash(Object key) {
  int h;
  // Fold high bits into low bucket bits.
  return key == null ? 0
    : (h = key.hashCode()) ^ (h >>> 16);
}
```

**Resizing.** Java resizes when the number of entries goes *above* a threshold: capacity times the maximum load factor. A default map has 16 buckets and a load factor of 0.75, so it holds 12 entries and doubles when the 13th is added.

Because the size is a power of two, doubling sends each entry in old bucket i either to bucket i or to bucket i + oldCapacity in the new table, depending on one bit of its hash (`hash & oldCap`). Java 8 uses this to split each chain into "low" and "high" lists in a single pass, preserving order.

**Tree bins (Java 8).** JEP 180 added protection against long chains. In OpenJDK 21, ordinary `put` invokes treeification when adding a ninth node to a chain of eight (`TREEIFY_THRESHOLD` is 8). Other insertion paths can reach the threshold differently. A tree bin gives logarithmic lookup when hashes or a consistent comparable-key order distinguish keys. Two conditions apply:

- If the whole table has fewer than **64** buckets (`MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY`), Java resizes the table instead, since a small table is the likelier cause of the long chain.
- When a resize splits a tree bin and a part has **6** or fewer entries (`UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD`), it turns back into a list. The gap between 8 and 6 avoids flipping back and forth.

Tree nodes are ordered by hash, then by `compareTo` if the keys are `Comparable`. For keys with identical hashes that are not comparable, the tree cannot order them meaningfully, so the guarantee is weaker; `String` keys, the usual flooding target, are comparable.

> [!example] How rare are tree bins?
> The HashMap source notes that with random hash codes and a default maximum load factor of 0.75, bucket sizes follow a **Poisson distribution** with mean about 0.5. Under that approximate model, the probability of exactly 8 entries is about 0.00000006 (see the reference maths below); this is not a measured treeification rate. Tree bins are a defence against bad or malicious hashes, not a normal-case optimisation.

The Poisson distribution gives the chance of seeing exactly k events when they happen independently at an average rate λ. Here an "event" is a key landing in a particular bucket:

```formula reference
P(k) = e^(−λ) λ^k / k!
where
P(k): the probability that a given bucket holds exactly k entries
k: the number of entries in the bucket
λ: lambda, the average number of entries per bucket, about 0.5 in the HashMap source's model
e: Euler's number, about 2.718
!: factorial, the product of all whole numbers from 1 up to that one; 8! = 40,320
^: "to the power of"
In words: with an average of half an entry per bucket, the chance of a bucket reaching 8 entries by luck is about 6 in 100 million, so a tree bin almost always signals a bad or hostile hash.
```

## Key takeaways
- Hash spreading folds high bits into low bucket bits.
- Doubling separates old chains by one additional hash bit.
- Tree-bin bounds need distinguishable hashes or comparable ordering; small tables resize first.

## Further reading
- [HashMap — Java SE 21 API docs](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/HashMap.html)
- [JEP 180: Handle Frequent HashMap Collisions with Balanced Trees](https://openjdk.org/jeps/180)
- [OpenJDK 21 HashMap source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openjdk/jdk21u/master/src/java.base/share/classes/java/util/HashMap.java)

options.explanation: It stays at 5 only if the bit worth 16 in its hash is 0. For 53 that bit is set.

options.text: Bucket 10
options.explanation: Doubling does not double the index. The new index is the hash's low 5 bits.

options.text: Bucket 21
options.explanation: Correct. Masking with thirty-one selects bucket twenty-one, the old bucket five plus old capacity sixteen, because the newly exposed bit is set.

options.text: Bucket 53
options.explanation: The index must be below the table size (32). It is the hash masked with 31, not the raw hash.

questions.workedExample:
1. With a power-of-two table, the bucket is the hash's low bits: the low 4 bits for 16 buckets, the low 5 bits for 32.
2. 53 is 110101 in binary. Its low 4 bits, 0101, give bucket 5 in the old table. Its low 5 bits, 10101, give bucket 21 in the new one.
3. The only new bit is bit 4 (worth 16). For 53 it is set (`53 & 16` is 16), so the entry moves from bucket 5 to 5 + 16 = 21. Had that bit been 0, it would have stayed in bucket 5.
4. Every entry in old bucket i therefore goes to i or i + 16. Java 8 splits each chain into a "lo" list and a "hi" list in one pass, without recomputing any hashes.

questions.prompt: In OpenJDK 21, a HashMap has 32 buckets and a chain of eight entries. An ordinary put adds a ninth distinct key to that chain. What happens?

options.text: The chain is converted into a red–black tree
options.explanation: Only if the table has at least 64 buckets (`MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY`). At 32, Java assumes the table is simply too small.

options.text: The table doubles to 64 buckets instead of treeifying
options.explanation: Correct. `treeifyBin` checks the table size first; below 64 it calls `resize()`, which may also split the long chain across two buckets.

options.text: Nothing: chains are only treeified when they reach 64 entries
options.explanation: 64 is the minimum *table* capacity for treeifying. The chain threshold is 8.

options.text: The map throws an exception to signal a bad hash function
options.explanation: Java never rejects keys for colliding; it degrades gracefully.

questions.workedExample:
1. The ordinary putVal path invokes treeifyBin when appending to a chain that already has eight nodes.
2. `treeifyBin` first checks: is `table.length < MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY` (64)? Here 32 < 64.
3. So it resizes to 64 buckets. Entries in the long chain split between bucket i and i + 32 according to one more hash bit.
4. If the chain is still 8+ long once the table has 64 or more buckets (e.g. all keys share the same full hash), the next insert into it converts it to a tree, giving O(log n) lookups for comparable keys, where n is the number of entries in that bin.

lessons.title: Java HashMap capacity planning
lessons.summary: A HashMap's capacity argument is not its entry limit; size for count divided by load factor, or use HashMap.newHashMap.
lessons.body:
A `HashMap` constructor's capacity argument is not the number of entries the map can hold. Plan for the threshold after power-of-two rounding, or let Java do the calculation for you.

## Pre-sizing a Java HashMap

`new HashMap<>(1000)` rounds the capacity up to the next power of two, 1,024, but at the default load factor of 0.75 its threshold is only 768 entries. It therefore still doubles once before reaching 1,000 entries. To hold a planned number of entries without any doubling, the threshold must be at least that number, so the capacity must be at least the entry count divided by the load factor:

```formula reference
C ≥ n / L
where
C: the capacity (buckets) to request, which Java rounds up to a power of two
n: the number of entries you plan to store
L: the maximum load factor, 0.75 by default
≥: "is at least"
In words: ask for at least the planned entry count divided by the load factor. For 1,000 entries at 0.75 that means a capacity of 1,334 or more, which Java rounds up to 2,048 buckets with a threshold of 1,536.
```

Java 19 added `HashMap.newHashMap(n)`, which does that calculation for you: `HashMap.newHashMap(1000)` gives 2,048 buckets.

## What happens without pre-sizing

A default map starts at 16 buckets, allocating its array lazily on the first insert; that first allocation is not a doubling. Its thresholds then run 12, 24, 48, 96, 192, 384, 768. Loading 1,000 distinct keys crosses all seven, so the map doubles seven times, rehashing everything present each time, and ends with 2,048 buckets. That is the same final size a pre-sized map starts with, reached through seven pauses.

A larger load factor raises the threshold, so capacity planning must include the constructor's second argument: `new HashMap<>(1000, 1.0f)` holds 1,000 entries in 1,024 buckets without doubling, at the price of slightly longer chains.

Pre-sizing does not make every `put` constant-time: building keys, hashing, equality, allocation and adversarial collisions remain separate costs, and collision-triggered resizes can still affect a small table before its ordinary size threshold. Use the factory when you know the expected entry count, and an explicit capacity when you deliberately need to control the bucket count and load policy. If entries are continually removed, plan for the peak number alive at once, not a cumulative daily count.

## Key takeaways
- Capacity arguments and expected entry counts are different.
- Include the load factor and power-of-two rounding when planning capacity.
- Pre-sizing avoids planned load-triggered doublings, without guaranteeing every operation’s latency.

## Further reading
- [HashMap — Java SE 21 API docs](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/HashMap.html)
- [JEP 180: Handle Frequent HashMap Collisions with Balanced Trees](https://openjdk.org/jeps/180)
- [OpenJDK 21 HashMap source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openjdk/jdk21u/master/src/java.base/share/classes/java/util/HashMap.java)

lessons.title: Two-sum and complement lookup
lessons.summary: For each number, look up the one partner that completes the target in a map of earlier values, turning a quadratic pair search into one pass.
lessons.body:
Many problems that look like they need two nested loops have an O(n) solution (n being the length of the input) that walks the input once while a hash map remembers what it has seen. The trade is always the same: spend O(n) memory to turn "search everything I've seen so far" (O(n) each time) into "look it up" (O(1) on average).

These bounds assume expected constant-time hash operations and bounded-cost arithmetic and equality. The units that follow cover the other recurring shapes; recognising *what the map remembers* matters more than memorising a particular loop.

## 1. Complement lookup: two-sum

> Given `nums` and `target`, return the indices of two numbers that add up to `target`.

A brute-force search checks every pair: O(n²) for an array of n numbers. The insight: for each number, the partner you need is fixed. It is the target minus the current number, its complement. If the target is 9 and you are looking at 2, only a 7 can complete the pair, so you need one lookup, not a search.

Instead of searching for the complement, ask a map whether you have already seen it.

```python
def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}  # value -> index
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if target - x in seen:
            return seen[target - x], i
        # Store after checking: no
        # self-pair.
        seen[x] = i
    return None

two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9)  # (0, 1)
two_sum([3, 3], 6)          # (0, 1)
```

Two details matter:

- **Check before you insert.** With `[3, 2, 4]` and target 6, inserting first would let `3` match itself. Checking first means `seen` only ever contains *earlier* elements.
- **Duplicates are fine.** For `[3, 3]`, the first 3 is stored; the second finds it.

Time O(n), space O(n). If the array is already sorted, two pointers from both ends solve it in O(1) extra space, which is the usual follow-up question.

The same "have I seen the complement?" shape solves: pairs with a given difference (look up `x - k` and `x + k`), "does any duplicate exist?" (complement is `x` itself), and "duplicate within distance k" (store each value's last index).

## Key takeaways
- Check the complement before recording the current value.
- The map must contain only earlier input indices.
- Duplicates can form a pair when they occur at distinct positions.

## Further reading
- [Time complexity of Python operations — Python wiki](https://wiki.python.org/moin/TimeComplexity)
- [Hash table — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_table)

Correct. 3 needs 3 (not seen yet), store it. 2 needs 4 (not seen), store it. 4 needs 2, which is at index 1: return (1, 2).
3 + 4 = 7, not 6. Index 0 would only pair with another 3.

options.text: It runs in O(n) time on average with O(n) extra space
